a10.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a10.speech: "There's no time set, but it could be very soon," ; "It'll be soon; we'll see what happens,"

a10.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a10.speech: Said he believes that Putin wants to end the war: "They have a big powerful machine, you understand that. They defeated Hitler and they defeated Napoleon. They've been fighting a long time," ; "They've done it before. But I think he would like to stop fighting." ; asked if he believes Putin wants to seize all of Ukraine's territory, said he had asked his Russian counterpart the same question and it would be a "big problem for us" if so.

a10.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a10.speech: Said that Putin had expressed his desire for peace in his phone call with Trump last week, even as he cautioned that the conflict would not be resolved overnight. "Now, obviously, it has to be followed up by action. So, the next few weeks and days will determine whether it's serious or not," ; "Ultimately, one phone call does not make peace. One phone call does not solve a war as complex as this one."

a10.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a10.speech: Said the specifics of the talks, including the makeup of the Russian delegation, had not been finalised: "I don't have any details for you this morning, other than to say that we stand ready to follow the president's lead on this and begin to explore ways, if those opportunities present itself, to begin a process towards peace," ; stressed that Ukraine and Europe would both have to be involved in any "real negotiations" that result from the meeting.

a10.speaker: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President
a10.speech: Said he would "never accept" any agreement reached without his country's involvement. "This is the war in Ukraine, against us, and it's our human losses,"

a10.speaker: Kaja Kallas, European foreign policy chief
a10.speech: "As I stand here in Munich tonight, I cannot help but ask, have we been here before? Czechoslovakia,1938," ; "We have an aggressor at our door intent on taking the land that isn't his. And the negotiators, not us, are already giving away their bargaining chips before the negotiations have even begun."

a10.speaker: Keir Starmer, UK Prime Minister
a10.speech: Said he is "ready and willing" to send British troops to Ukraine to help keep the peace in the event of a deal to end the war. "I do not say that lightly," ; "I feel very deeply the responsibility that comes with potentially putting British servicemen and women in harm's way." ; "But any role in helping to guarantee Ukraine's security is helping to guarantee the security of our continent and the security of this country," ; "The end of this war, when it comes, cannot merely become a temporary pause before Putin attacks again."

a77.speaker: Yury Ushakov, Russian presidential adviser
a77.speech: Confirmed on Tuesday that reports of Steve Witkoff's upcoming visit to Russia are accurate.

a77.speaker: Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary
a77.speech: Told journalists that both Trump and Witkoff "wanted everybody to know that the negotiations continue." "We feel, again, we are hopefully moving in the right direction, and the special envoy Steve Witkoff will be heading to Russia again later this week to continue talks with Vladimir Putin."

a77.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokesperson
a77.speech: Said Secretary of State Marco Rubio will not attend the latest round of talks due to his "busy" schedule; Washington will instead be represented by General Keith Kellogg.

a77.speaker: The Washington Post (report)
a77.speech: Reported that US proposals could include formally recognizing Crimea as Russian territory and potentially lifting sanctions on Moscow.

a77.speaker: The Financial Times (report)
a77.speech: Claimed Russia is prepared to halt hostilities along the current front lines; separately reported that Witkoff would skip a meeting with European and Ukrainian officials to visit Moscow instead.

a77.speaker: Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesman
a77.speech: Warned that "a lot of fakes are being published now, including by respected publications," and urged the public to rely on official sources regarding developments in US-Russia talks on the Ukraine conflict.

a77.speaker: Russia (government statement)
a77.speech: Has stated that any peace deal must address the "root causes" of the conflict, including NATO's eastward expansion and Kiev's aspirations to join the US-led bloc, and has demanded that Kiev recognize Crimea, the Donetsk and Lugansk People's Republics, and the regions of Kherson and Zaporozhye as part of Russia.

a219.speaker: Emerse Fae, coach of the Ivory Coast national football team
a219.speech: At a press conference on Wednesday 27 August 2025, explained the conditions under which the player is joining his squad for the last two World Cup qualifying matches, and was full of praise for Alban Lafont while presenting his list: "He is a great goalkeeper who is very good on his line. He has a lot of experience. His calm and composure will do the other young goalkeepers and the squad good. Given Yaya's situation, Alban's arrival will calm him. I think he will really bring us something."

a219.speaker: Emerse Fae, coach of the Ivory Coast national football team
a219.speech: On the question of the player's sporting nationality (Burkinabe through his mother and French through his father), reassured: "We take care of everything administrative. If we have selected him, it is because administratively he is Ivorian. Otherwise, we would not have allowed ourselves to select him. He is Ivorian."

a219.speaker: Emerse Fae, coach of the Ivory Coast national football team
a219.speech: Detailed: "For his selection, he is a goalkeeper who has experience, a goalkeeper who will bring us a lot, even at the level of the group. He is a quality goalkeeper. Since he arrived at Panathinaikos he has not played, but he has had a very good pre-season. He is in his legs. He is in form. He is a player who is very happy to join us and very eager to join us in the national team. He is due to start in the league next weekend."

a219.speaker: Emerse Fae, coach of the Ivory Coast national football team
a219.speech: Was clear on whether Lafont's arrival was meant to make him number 1, concluding: "It does not necessarily reshuffle the cards. In our discussions, we were very clear with him. He agrees with our project. He comes in all humility. He does not come with the pretension of becoming number 1. No. He will discover his new environment. He will discover the group. He comes with his experience. So Yaya will remain our number 1."

a510.speaker: Victor Nyasulu, ZAMMSA director-general
a510.speech: Featuring on Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation's Special Interview programme on Thursday night, revealed the agency's blueprint to make itself 100 percent capable of distributing medicines and medical supplies across Zambia: "We don't like the fact that at the moment, distribution is helped 70 percent by USAID. We are working out a plan to make sure that we are ready to do 100 percent as ZAMMSA."

a510.speaker: World Health Organisation (standard cited)
a510.speech: Cited as the yardstick against which ZAMMSA's attainment of 70 percent drugs in its central storage facility in Lusaka is measured.

a541.speaker: FAO GIEWS (Global Information and Early Warning System) Country Brief on Mozambique
a541.speech: Reports that cereal production in 2022 is estimated at a below-average level of 2.6 million tonnes as adverse weather conditions and the impact of conflicts curtail crop yields and cause localised crop losses; that cereal import requirements in 2022/23 are forecast to rise to an above-average 1.7 million tonnes, 13 percent more than the previous five-year average; that elevated global prices of energy and foods are pushing up domestic prices, with annual food inflation estimated at 10 percent in June 2022, up from 8 percent in January 2022; and that worsening conflict, high prices and localized shortfalls in crop production are foreseen to amplify humanitarian needs in 2022/23, with the number of people in need of food assistance expected to rise above the 1.86 million estimated in 2021/22.

a541.speaker: FAO geospatial analysis
a541.speech: According to it, Cyclone Gombe alone resulted in an estimated 20,500 hectares of cropland in Zambezia and Nampula provinces (less than 5 percent of the area planted with cereals) being inundated.

a541.speaker: IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification)
a541.speech: The IPC acute food insecurity forecast for the peak lean period between December 2022 and March 2023 is not yet available.

a541.speaker: FAO (disclaimer)
a541.speech: "The designations employed and the presentation of material in this information product do not imply the expression of any opinion whatsoever on the part of FAO concerning the legal status of any country, territory, city or area or of its authorities, or concerning the delimitation of its frontiers or boundaries."

a632.speaker: APP-Sobeyaa Party (press statement)
a632.speech: Issued a powerful call for immediate action to address the escalating housing crisis in Sukuta Salagi, condemned the demolitions, highlighting the severe humanitarian and legal implications, emphasized that rising costs of essential goods and soaring urban rent prices have made it nearly impossible for displaced residents to secure alternative housing, pointed to serious legal violations, and proposed a six-point plan: an immediate halt to demolitions for a comprehensive review; fair compensation as required by law; inclusive dialogue with all stakeholders, including affected residents; public disclosure of relevant documentation to ensure transparency; comprehensive land reform to prevent future disputes; and temporary measures to alleviate the suffering of displaced families. The party vowed to collaborate with stakeholders to uphold justice and good governance.

a632.speaker: Essa Mbye Faal, Secretary General and Party Leader of APP-Sobeyaa
a632.speech: “The humanitarian impact of these demolitions is significant and far-reaching” ; “As a party committed to constitutional democracy and social justice, we believe these challenges require solutions that prioritise both legal compliance and human dignity.”

a632.speaker: Edward Francis Small Centre for Rights and Justice
a632.speech: Raised concerns about serious legal violations in the demolitions, which the APP-Sobeyaa Party echoed.

a632.speaker: The Gambia's 1997 Constitution, Section 22 (cited)
a632.speech: Guarantees property rights and mandates “prompt payment of fair and adequate compensation” for any compulsory land acquisition.

a632.speaker: Land Acquisition and Compensation Act (Cap 57:06) (cited)
a632.speech: Further enshrines protections of property rights and compensation.

a632.speaker: Affected residents of Sukuta Salagi
a632.speech: Many claim they built their homes on land legally acquired or inherited, only to face abrupt eviction without adequate notice or compensation; residents report receiving neither compensation nor transparent explanations for the demolitions, and argue the process was unjust and lacked proper legal grounding.

a632.speaker: Ministry of Lands, Regional Government, and Religious Affairs
a632.speech: Has defended the demolitions as necessary to reclaim public space.

a635.speaker: Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
a635.speech: Decided to allocate to Cote d'Ivoire an additional 4.4 million US dollars (2.6 billion CFA francs) under the “Regional Energy Compact” Programme approved on 18 September 2024, in order to facilitate the development of the programme.

a635.speaker: SERCOM (communication service, source of the report)
a635.speech: Source of the report on the signing of the Amendment to the Compact Development Fund and the additional MCC allocation to Cote d'Ivoire.

a797.speaker: David Christian, historian and researcher
a797.speech: Affirmed that the sharing of knowledge and cooperation among human beings is the way to sustain life on the face of planet Earth, considering that uniting human efforts and goals is a task borne by all leaders around the world in order to close the gaps between states in order to build the future.

a797.speaker: David Christian, historian and researcher
a797.speech: Said that "modern human ideas are similar to a certain extent; at the beginning of this year, 2024, the majority of the world's countries agreed to reduce the proportion of greenhouse gas emissions in order to preserve our planet, and this international consensus is another example of the similarity of peoples." ; Added that "sharing knowledge with neighbouring communities pushed us to innovate the sustainability of life on the planet, after enriching it gradually," but considered that the forced merging of cultures led to bloody conflicts that created a pessimistic image for many human beings.

a797.speaker: David Christian, historian and researcher
a797.speech: Addressed the danger of human activities on Earth, saying: "200 years ago humans discovered the energy locked in fossil fuels and used it to transform the surface of planet Earth, so we changed its shape and its oceans, and this is something that has not happened for millions of years; then we learned to make weapons of mass destruction, and that means that we are living at a turning point in the life of the planet and we as humans dominate its fate, and at the same time we pose a danger to it."

a860.speaker: Philip Agbese, member of the Nigerian House of Representatives
a860.speech: Moved a motion expressing concern that despite the massive inflow of donor funds, Nigeria continues to record one of the highest disease burdens in the world; he noted that Nigeria received $1.8 billion from the Global Fund for HIV, TB and malaria response between 2021 and 2025, and another $2.8 billion from USAID for health threats including HIV, malaria, polio and TB between 2022 and 2024, and added that the country also benefitted from over $6 billion in health assistance from PEPFAR within the same period.

a860.speaker: Philip Agbese, member of the Nigerian House of Representatives
a860.speech: Lamented that despite these huge investments, the nation's health outcomes remain dire: "In 2023, approximately 15,000 AIDS-related deaths occurred among Nigerian children aged 0–14, while a total of 51,000 AIDS-related deaths were recorded nationwide" ; He further pointed out that Nigeria ranks third globally in HIV deaths, first in Africa and sixth worldwide in tuberculosis burden, and bears the highest malaria burden globally, accounting for about 26.6 percent of global malaria cases and 31 percent of malaria deaths.

a860.speaker: Philip Agbese, member of the Nigerian House of Representatives
a860.speech: Said the lack of a "coordinated and robust oversight" of implementing agencies by the National Assembly may have contributed to the poor results despite billions in funding; citing Sections 88 and 89 of the 1999 Constitution (as amended), he said the legislature has the constitutional power to summon any ministry, agency or non-governmental organisation for accountability in the utilisation of public or donor funds.

a860.speaker: Philip Agbese, member of the Nigerian House of Representatives
a860.speech: Warned that unless drastic steps are taken to reevaluate how donor funds are managed, Nigeria risks failing to meet the UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of eliminating HIV, TB, and malaria by 2030.

a860.speaker: Nigerian House of Representatives (resolution/motion)
a860.speech: Resolved on Tuesday to direct its Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria Control to investigate the utilisation of over $4.6 billion in foreign grants received from the Global Fund and USAID between 2021 and 2025: "To mandate the House Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria Control to investigate the utilisation of the grants received by Nigeria from 2021 to 2025 for the fight against HIV, Tuberculosis and Malaria, and report back to the House within four weeks for further legislative action. Mandate the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare to provide the implementation plan and approvals granted by the National Assembly for the utilisation and expenditure of these grants."

a951.speaker: US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
a951.speech: On May 27, in a ceremony at Outapi in the Omusati region, outlined the expansion of this support from 14 to 18 districts in eight regions, adding 20 000 new beneficiaries so far this year.

a951.speaker: Daniel Lee, Acting USAID health office director
a951.speech: “This work is an important contribution towards achieving HIV epidemic control through a comprehensive response for families that provide community-based treatment, care and support interventions to children and their caregivers that are living with or are affected by HIV” ; “PEPFAR will continue funding OVC programmes with over US$4 million this year – or N$56 million – to ensure that OVC services are continued and expanded in 18 districts.”

a1015.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1015.speech: Stressed in a statement that USAID had not fulfilled its objectives since the end of the Cold War and had created a network of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) that lived "at the expense of American taxpayers" ; "This era of inefficiency has officially come to an end. Under the Trump administration, we will finally have foreign aid that prioritises our national interests" ; said American citizens "should not pay taxes to finance bankrupt governments in distant countries" and promised that from now on "aid will be targeted and limited in time."

a1015.speaker: Humanitarian aid experts and international organisations
a1015.speech: Heavily criticised the end of USAID, warning that its disappearance leaves an enormous gap in health, education and humanitarian crisis response programmes.

a1015.speaker: Barack Obama and George W. Bush, former US presidents
a1015.speech: Levelled rare criticism at the Trump government on Monday, at a farewell event for the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).

a1015.speaker: Study coordinated by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), published in The Lancet
a1015.speech: Warned that the cuts to US aid could lead to more than 14 million 'preventable' deaths by 2030 ; according to the study, USAID had a fundamental impact in reducing mortality from HIV/AIDS, malaria and neglected tropical diseases worldwide.

a1190.speaker: Rev. Dr Fred Deegbe, Board Chairman of the Coalition of Domestic Election Observers (CODEO)
a1190.speech: Said CODEO has deployed 4,000 election observers across the country to monitor the 2024 Presidential and Parliamentary elections; explained that 3,401 Rapid Response Observers will be stationed at a representative sample of CODEO stations in all 276 constituencies across the 16 regions of Ghana, including 1,500 Private Voter Tabulation Observers (PVT) and 1,000 Youth Observers. "The Rapid Response Observers will include 307 CODEO Regional Coordinators and Constituency Supervisors. The Roaming Observers will be at all 276 constituencies where voting will occur. In addition, members of the CODEO Advisory Board and the CODEO General Assembly will undertake roaming observations in various constituencies." ; "For the first time, CODEO will also have 16 observer stations at the 16 regional coalition centres of the Electoral Commission while two observers will also be deployed to the National Coalition Centre in Accra." ; "CODEO leverages statistical principles to select polling stations for its Rapid Response Observers. The deployment and observation plan ensures an issue-wide presence and visibility in every region and constituency, including remote and hard-to-reach areas."

a1190.speaker: Rev. Dr Fred Deegbe, Board Chairman of CODEO
a1190.speech: Outlined the intensive preparations undertaken by the Coalition prior to the final day of election, including recruitment and training of 276 constituency supervisors nationwide in November. "Finally, in November, the Coalition recruited and trained Podium station rapid response observers. Every recruited observer received training in election and election observation, including the legal framework for elections, election day procedures, election observation and tools of observation, as well as the code of conduct for election observers." ; "To ensure their adequate preparation, officials from the Electoral Commission facilitated training in the voting processes. CODEO observers were recruited mainly from its member organisations, as well as selected youth-focused organisations." ; "Ladies and gentlemen, with all these preparatory efforts successfully executed, we are confident that our observers have received the highest quality of training and are ready to carry out this important national assignment."

a1226.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a1226.speech: has warned that almost 14 million people in countries including Afghanistan, Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan risk severe hunger due to cuts in global humanitarian aid.

a1226.speaker: WFP report, “A Lifeline at Risk”
a1226.speech: estimated that cuts to its food assistance could push 13.7 million people from “crisis” to “emergency” levels of hunger, one step away from famine in a five-level international hunger scale.

a1226.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
a1226.speech: said major WFP operations in six countries - Afghanistan, Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan - are facing serious funding shortages before the end of the year.

a1226.speaker: WFP spokesperson (anonymous)
a1226.speech: clarified on Thursday that the expected 13.7-million increase in the number of severely hungry people included, but was “not exclusive”, to those six countries.

a1226.speaker: Cindy McCain, WFP executive director
a1226.speech: said "The gap between what WFP needs to do and what we can afford to do has never been larger. We are at risk of losing decades of progress in the fight against hunger," ; "It's not just the countries engulfed in major emergencies. Even hard-won gains in the Sahel region, where 500,000 people have been lifted out of aid dependence, could experience severe setbacks without help, and we want to prevent that."

a1328.speaker: Thabani Masuku, undergraduate from Rhodes University (essay)
a1328.speech: Outlines the insidious nature of corruption and offers possible solutions. Argues that corruption gradually erodes governance structures and also poses a serious threat to the quality of life and livelihoods of the citizens in a country; that the existence of corruption in any country not only undermines social justice but also undermines the rule of law, therefore the significance of efforts to address and ultimately eliminate corruption cannot be overstated ; notes that corruption bears with it costs, to the state, economy and citizens, whose parameters and reach cannot be accurately defined because of the illegal nature of corrupt acts and transactions ; recommends that there should be a concerted effort towards establishing and enforcing laws against corruption so as to inspire and consolidate a sense of trust in the country's justice systems; that there must be a practical aspect of this justice that recovers all ill-gotten gains and restores them to the rightful owners or to the state; and that fiscal decentralisation would serve a great deal in addressing the incidences of corruption related to abuse of autonomy ; concludes that corruption affects all people and no one is exempt from the ravenous costs to the economic, political and social well-being of a country.

a1328.speaker: USAid research
a1328.speech: According to USAid research, the choice to engage in an act of corruption is largely decided by the perceived ratio between the benefits derived from the act of corruption and the penalties the perpetrator is likely to suffer in the event of exposure.

a1328.speaker: United Nations member states / United Nations Convention against Corruption
a1328.speech: In response to the growing rate of corruption, the member states of the United Nations convened and came up with the United Nations Convention against Corruption, a multilateral treaty promoted by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

a1328.speaker: Jason Kelbrick, undergraduate from Nelson Mandela University (essay)
a1328.speech: Explores corruption's destructive consequences and points to constructive remedies. States that along with corruption comes various economic and fiscal costs which have a direct effect on a country's allocation of resources and social welfare ; that countries with higher levels of corruption experience significantly lower government expenditure on key economic fundamentals such as education and health, exposing the country to further negative effects in areas such as GDP growth and foreign direct investment ; that a positive relationship emerges between corruption and income inequality, and that countries with more corruption experience weakened political institutions and a deficient court system leading to higher political instability ; that corruption increases inflation rates, tends to depreciate the real exchange rate, and encourages the development of the shadow economy, eroding government revenue ; that recent unscientific evidence demonstrates corruption in the public sector can increase the costs of services by 30% to 50% ; recommends promoting transparency and an ethical judicial system, reforming public administration and financial management, and fiscal decentralisation, concluding that a clear strategy such as the National Development Programme must be successfully implemented.

a1328.speaker: Bueno de Mesquita et al. (2001) (research)
a1328.speech: According to Bueno de Mesquita et al. (2001), a democratic governance system can actually facilitate growth as citizens are better able to remove corrupt politicians.

a1328.speaker: Khayelihle Madlopha, undergraduate from the University of Zululand (essay)
a1328.speech: Clearly outlines the devastating effects of corruption, describing its various guises as political corruption, bureaucratic corruption, legislative corruption and private sector corruption ; argues that corruption acts like a tax that discourages Foreign Direct Investments, and that corruption's negative effect on South Africa's total investment is indisputable, with local investors tending to "park" their big investment projects, as big industry players like Pioneer Foods and some big mining companies did after the most recent presidential Cabinet reshuffle ; argues corruption fuels poor service delivery, citing the lack of textbooks in Limpopo in 2012, and that poor government delivery hinders business growth ; argues widespread corruption undermines the culture of compliance, increasing tax evasion and eroding state revenue, and distorts government expenditure through cost inflation ; states it is estimated the country loses about R25 billion each year to corruption in government procurement, and that corruption has contributed to the large budget deficit (3.9% in 2016) and government debt (currently 51% of GDP) ; concludes: "corruption is a chronic economic and social ill that we must fight. Through collaborative work and dedication, we can do this. We must free our country from corruption and 'economic gangsters'."

a1328.speaker: Transparency International
a1328.speech: According to Transparency International, corruption is "one of the greatest challenges of the contemporary world", particularly for developing countries.

a1328.speaker: Business International's Corruption Index
a1328.speech: Indicates that more corrupt countries experienced significantly lower investment rates, because of a negative relationship between corruption and investments.

a1328.speaker: Economists (estimate cited)
a1328.speech: Economists have estimated that a corrupt country is likely to achieve aggregate investment levels of almost 5% less than a country that is relatively "incorrupt".

a1328.speaker: Grant Thornton survey
a1328.speech: In a Grant Thornton survey, 58% of executives interviewed indicated that they were delaying their business expansions in South Africa ; in 2016, 32% of private business owners surveyed by Grant Thornton identified poor service delivery relating to utilities (water and electricity) as having the greatest negative impact on their growth.

a1328.speaker: Corruption Watch
a1328.speech: Says corruption fuels poor service delivery, because huge amounts of money that could be used for service delivery are lost to corruption every year ; says corruption has far reaching effects on a country and its people and is central to many other issues a nation experiences.

a1328.speaker: Special Investigative Unit report (2011)
a1328.speech: Highlighted irregularities and wasteful expenditure within the education sector; the report also found that an R680-million contract was awarded to EduSolutions not because of the ability to provide the service but because of political connections.

a1328.speaker: Tanzi and Davoodi (researchers)
a1328.speech: In a study of 68 countries over the period 1980-1995, researchers Tanzi and Davoodi found a significant negative impact of corruption on state revenues.

a1328.speaker: Schalk Bothma, undergraduate from the University of Stellenbosch (essay)
a1328.speech: Unpacks the repercussions of rampant corruption, arguing that the massive discontent with rampant corruption is completely justified and that corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain ; argues corruption leads to lower rates of economic growth, indirect economic costs, inefficient public investment, reduced private and foreign direct investment, reduced entrepreneurial innovation, higher rates of inflation and increased income inequality ; argues its fiscal costs include losses due to corruption, a change in the composition of public expenditure away from health and education, lower tax revenue, and higher public debt and financing costs ; notes that the April downgrades of South Africa's foreign currency debt to sub-investment grade followed a controversial decision by President Jacob Zuma to fire Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan, in a Cabinet reshuffle deemed by many to be the product of cronyism ; concludes that the pervasiveness of the costs of corruption and its widespread consequences are clear, that those in poverty are hit the hardest, and that this creates a vicious cycle that can only be halted by uprooting corruption in its totality.

a1328.speaker: World Bank
a1328.speech: States it has corruption as "the single greatest obstacle to economic and social development".

a1328.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1328.speech: IMF research points out that an increase of 1 point in the corruption index can lead to a reduction in foreign investment by as much as 8% ; according to the IMF, annually a staggering $1.5 trillion is lost due to corruption worldwide, amounting to roughly 1.8% to 2% of global GDP ; according to the IMF, widespread corruption promotes a culture of non-compliance with taxation laws, thereby increasing tax evasion.

a1328.speaker: Parliamentary Monitoring Group
a1328.speech: Estimates the size of the corruption phenomenon in South Africa is about R25 billion annually.

a1338.speaker: Wall Street Journal (report)
a1338.speech: Reported that Talkie's Chinese counterpart, Xingye, was pulled from app stores due to explicit content and had to relaunch with strict content filters.

a1338.speaker: Experts on Chinese affairs
a1338.speech: Alleged that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has backed Talkie's rapid expansion into Western markets, and that the app carries hidden factors of China's unrestricted war against the West.

a1338.speaker: Tang Jingyuan, China affairs commentator and columnist
a1338.speech: Said he believed that the Chinese regime's influence has been instrumental in Talkie's rapid rise in the U.S. market.

a1338.speaker: MiniMax (Talkie's developer) - non-response
a1338.speech: There has been no explanation from MiniMax so far, leaving users and industry experts to speculate on the exact reasons behind the app's removal from the US iOS App Store.

a1338.speaker: Article in Toolify.ai
a1338.speech: According to the article, visitors could easily access numerous underage and child scenarios within the Talkie app; these interactions are "nothing short of an atrocity, making the app more of a child abuse simulator than a storytelling platform"; the app lacked responsibility and accountability from its developer, Subs Up Ltd., and the platform has zero checks and balances regarding the characters and content available for users to engage with. The article also stated that the app may be financially incentivized to cater to the desires and fantasies of its users, regardless of the ethical implications.

a1338.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a1338.speech: Said that a financial motive might be behind the luring content on Talkie, since the more users interact with underage characters, the more these characters are served to them.

a1338.speaker: Chinese industry analysts at the 2024 World Internet Conference (WIC) Wuzhen Summit
a1338.speech: Noted how Chinese emerging unicorns such as Shanghai-based MiniMax, Beijing-based Moonshot AI, and 01.AI were seizing new opportunities in the global market, seeking to leverage their peculiar strengths in AI innovations.

a1467.speaker: Local pro-democracy group in Sudan
a1467.speech: said on Saturday that at least 50 people were killed in central Sudan in an attack by the paramilitaries of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), who besieged entire villages in the area ; 50 people were killed and "more than 200 wounded" on Friday.

a1467.speaker: AFP
a1467.speech: recalls that since April 2023 the country has been the scene of a war between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by General Mohamed Hamdane Daglo, and the army led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhane, the country's de facto ruler, one of the poorest countries in the world.

a1467.speaker: Doctors (unnamed)
a1467.speech: according to doctors, the war has left tens of thousands dead, with estimates ranging from 20,000 to 150,000, most of the victims going unrecorded.

a1467.speaker: Hasaheisa Resistance Committee, pro-democracy group organising mutual aid among residents
a1467.speech: told AFP: "The villages of al-Sariha and Azraq (located in Al-Jazira State) are under attack" ; in al-Sariha, 50 people were killed and "more than 200 wounded" on Friday, and it was impossible "to evacuate the wounded (...) because of the shelling and snipers" of the RSF ; no toll could be given for the neighbouring village of Azraq, but the Committee said it was under "total siege, suffering the same violations as al-Sariha."

a1467.speaker: Sudanese doctors' union
a1467.speech: on Friday called on the United Nations to press for safe humanitarian corridors to the villages "that are facing genocide at the hands of the militia" of the RSF, rescue operations having become impossible.

a1467.speaker: Medical sources in several villages
a1467.speech: according to medical sources in several villages, almost all emergency care centres have been forced to close.

a1467.speaker: United Arab Emirates
a1467.speech: denies the allegations that it supports the RSF.

a1467.speaker: Minni Arcou Minnawi, governor of Sudan's Darfur region, a former rebel leader now close to the army
a1467.speech: accused neighbouring Chad of arming the paramilitaries.

a1467.speaker: Abderaman Koulamallah, Chad's Minister of Foreign Affairs and government spokesman
a1467.speech: Chad insisted on Thursday that it was not arming the paramilitaries: "Chad has no interest in amplifying the war in Sudan by supplying weapons, we are one of the few countries where this war has significant repercussions."

a1467.speaker: Catherine Pattillo, Deputy Director of the Africa Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1467.speech: told AFP this week that the war in Sudan risked causing serious economic damage to its already struggling neighbours: "Many of these neighbouring countries are already fragile and have their own challenges to meet. Now they face an influx of refugees, security issues, trade difficulties, which represents a real challenge for their growth."

a1467.speaker: United Nations
a1467.speech: according to the UN, the conflict has displaced more than ten million people.

a1497.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a1497.speech: "I would like to reiterate my words of appreciation, with a special thought for the Malian staff of MINUSMA. These staff lived through the government's decision to request the withdrawal of the UN Mission in the interest of our country... who experienced this withdrawal as a social and financial trauma, but who also received this decision with a sense of dignity and responsibility that I wanted to salute," he stated. ; For him, this final phase is full of symbolism, lessons and opportunities for better envisaging the appropriate format for United Nations intervention in our country.

a1497.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a1497.speech: "MINUSMA had symbolised in the eyes of Malians what the international community, through the United Nations, had best to offer: peace and stability," recalled the head of Malian diplomacy. And he stressed that the handover of MINUSMA's last site coincides with the anniversary of the recapture of Kidal by the FAMa.

a1497.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a1497.speech: "It thus became obvious that the Mission, in its form, did not meet the requirements on the ground," regretted Minister Diop, who added that while the Mission, in its first year, contributed to consolidating the FAMa's hold over areas liberated from terrorist occupation, successive developments showed the limits of its intervention.

a1497.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Malian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a1497.speech: Pointed out that the end of MINUSMA's presence does not mean the end of cooperation between Mali and the United Nations. "Cooperation between our country and the United Nations existed before MINUSMA's arrival and continues at least as much, if not better, since its departure, thanks to the experience and expertise of the United Nations country teams in Mali," he noted. ; "MINUSMA was an important mechanism in Mali's cooperation with the United Nations, but I am happy to acknowledge and salute the excellent articulation between the government's vision and the actions on the ground of the United Nations Funds, Agencies and Programmes operating in Mali," he acknowledged.

a1497.speaker: Atul Khare, UN Under-Secretary-General for Operational Support
a1497.speech: announced that a new chapter focused on humanitarian affairs would be opened. "We are closing one chapter and opening another... a chapter focused on strengthening United Nations support to Mali in the areas of humanitarian aid and development. The United Nations remains committed alongside Mali during this transition and to support Mali's continued efforts towards development and prosperity," indicated Atul Khare.

a1513.speaker: Ignatius Kariseb, Chairperson of the Omaheke Regional Council
a1513.speech: Has called on the residents, particularly farmers, to desist from evicting employees because of disagreements.

a1570.speaker: Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, President of the Southwest State of Somalia, and Richard H. Riley, US Ambassador to Somalia
a1570.speech: Both leaders emphasized the importance of continued collaboration to ensure the success of the U.S.-backed development projects in the Southwest State, which are critical to fostering economic growth, improving infrastructure, and delivering essential services to the local population.

a1570.speaker: Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, President of the Southwest State of Somalia, and Richard H. Riley, US Ambassador to Somalia
a1570.speech: Underscored the need for sustained dialogue and cooperation among Somali leaders to address ongoing challenges and advance the country's democratic processes.

a1570.speaker: Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, President of the Southwest State of Somalia, and Richard H. Riley, US Ambassador to Somalia
a1570.speech: Both parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening stability in the Southwest region, discussing measures to combat threats posed by armed groups and to create a safer environment for residents and development activities.

a1621.speaker: Yemeni recruits who travelled to Russia
a1621.speech: Told the Financial Times they were promised high salaried employment and even Russian citizenship; when they arrived with the help of a Houthi-linked company, they were then forcibly inducted into the Russian army and sent to the front lines in Ukraine.

a1621.speaker: US diplomats
a1621.speech: Say the entente between the Kremlin and the Houthis, unimaginable before the war in Ukraine, is a sign of how far Russia is willing to go to extend that conflict into new theatres including the Middle East; they have said Moscow provides a range of help to Houthis, including targeting data for some missile launches, and has been discussing arms sales, including advanced anti-ship missiles.

a1621.speaker: Tim Lenderking, US special envoy for Yemen (on Russia-Houthi contacts and weapons)
a1621.speech: Confirmed Russia is actively pursuing contacts with the Houthis and discussing weapons transfers, though he declined to be more specific: "We know that there are Russian personnel in Sana'a helping to deepen this dialogue. The kinds of weapons that are being discussed are very alarming, and would enable the Houthis to better target ships in the Red Sea and possibly beyond." ; "We've seen report that there are discussions around [anti-ship missiles] and other types of lethal equipment that would augment what the Houthis are already able to do."

a1621.speaker: Tim Lenderking, US special envoy for Yemen (on recruitment of Yemeni mercenaries)
a1621.speech: Said he had seen reports: "I would say that it definitely concerns us. It is part of this trend, and it's not something that would necessarily surprise us."

a1621.speaker: Maged Almadhaji, head of the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies
a1621.speech: Said Russia too is taking an interest "in any group in the Red Sea, or in the Middle East, that is hostile to the US"; he said that the mercenaries are organised by the Houthis as part of an effort to build links to Russia.

a1621.speaker: A spokesman for Ansar Allah (official name for the Houthi movement)
a1621.speech: Did not respond to a request for comment.

a1621.speaker: Mohammed al Bukhaiti, member of the Ansar Allah politburo
a1621.speech: Told the Russian news website Meduza earlier this month that they were in "constant contact" with the Russian leadership "to develop these relations in all areas, including economics, politics and the military."

a1621.speaker: Farea al Muslimi, expert on the Gulf region at Chatham House
a1621.speech: Said few of the Yemeni mercenaries have any training and many do not want to be there: "One thing Russia needs is soldiers, and it's clear the Houthis are recruiting, [for them]," describing it as an overture to Moscow. "Yemen is a pretty easy place to recruit. It is a very poor country."

a1621.speaker: Contracts signed by the Yemenis, seen by the Financial Times
a1621.speech: Listed a company founded by Abdulwali Abdo Hassan al-Jabri, a prominent Houthi politician; one enlistment contract was dated July 3, and was countersigned by the head of a selection centre for contract soldiers in the city of Nizhnii Novgorod.

a1621.speaker: Al Jabri company registration documents (Salalah, Oman)
a1621.speech: Identify the company as a tour operator and retail supplier of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals.

a1621.speaker: Nabil (pseudonym), Yemeni recruit
a1621.speech: Estimated that he was part of a group of around 200 Yemenis conscripted into the Russian army in September after arriving in Moscow; said that while some were experienced fighters, many had no military training, and that they were tricked into travelling to Russia and signed enlistment contracts they could not read; said he was lured by promises of lucrative employment in fields such as "security" and "engineering," hoping to earn enough to complete his studies.

a1621.speaker: Yemeni men in a video shared with the Financial Times
a1621.speech: "We are under bombardment. Mines, drones, digging bunkers," said one of the men, adding that one colleague had attempted suicide and been taken to a hospital; the men said they were carrying wooden planks through a mine-infested forest, apparently to build a bomb shelter: "We don't even get five minutes to rest, we are so tired." Another message sent a few days later said they had no winter clothes.

a1621.speaker: Nabil's uncle, who lives in the UK
a1621.speech: Said last week his nephew was recently injured and in hospital, but was unable to share more details.

a1621.speaker: Abdullah (pseudonym), Yemeni recruit
a1621.speech: Said he was promised a $10,000 bonus and $2,000 per month, plus eventual Russian citizenship, to work in Russia manufacturing drones; arriving in Moscow on September 18, he said his group was forcibly taken from the airport to a facility five hours from Moscow where a man, speaking in simple Arabic, fired a pistol over their heads when they refused to sign the enlistment contract, which was in Russian: "I signed it because I was scared." ; said many of the original group of arrivals died in Ukraine, brought to the war by "scammers who traffic in human beings": "It was all a lie."

a1621.speaker: Al Jabri General Trading & Investment Co SPC
a1621.speech: Did not respond to several phone calls and emails sent to the address listed on its corporate registration documents; Al Jabri, its founder, was also unreachable on his phone number.

a1621.speaker: Ahmed Salem Wahishi, Yemen's ambassador to Moscow
a1621.speech: Referred questions about the Russian army's recruitment of Yemenis to the embassy's military attaché, who did not respond to phone calls and messages.

a1621.speaker: Ali Al-Subahi, chair of the board of the International Federation of Yemeni Migrants
a1621.speech: Said "this is a humanitarian issue that unites all Yemenis, regardless of political affiliation"; he stressed that hundreds of Yemenis are still in Russia: "We are following up on their removal from the battlefields."

a1739.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1739.speech: Identified USAID's abrupt 90-day pause in services without prior notice as the most critical issue currently facing Ghana's health sector, speaking during his maiden State of the Nation Address on Thursday, February 27, 2025, in Accra; expressed concern over the potential withdrawal of USAID programmes that may not align with the United States' strategic interests; said the disruption would severely impact critical health programmes, particularly the delivery of medical commodities to regional medical stores and healthcare facilities in the Upper West, Upper East, Northern and Savannah regions, and that USAID's support for the National HIV/AIDS Control Programme, including the provision of antiretroviral therapies (ARTs) in the Western, Western North and Ahafo regions, is now in jeopardy.

a1739.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana
a1739.speech: Emphasized the potential devastating consequences of the withdrawal and assured the public that urgent steps would be taken, revealing that he had directed the Minister for Finance to make immediate financial arrangements to counter the loss of USAID support: "The impact will be devastating without urgent intervention. I have therefore directed the Minister for Finance to make immediate financial arrangements to mitigate this loss, and I expect that this will be reflected in his budget, which will be presented next month."

a1743.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) (statement/communique)
a1743.speech: Warned on Wednesday that living conditions for refugees in the Gambella region of western Ethiopia are deteriorating rapidly because of a drastic reduction in humanitarian aid, which it said is mainly linked to a decline in funding from the main international donors, notably USAID, seriously jeopardising essential services such as food distribution and access to health care, drinking water and sanitation: "The major cuts in humanitarian aid are causing a rapid deterioration in the living conditions of refugees in the Gambella region." ; described a critical situation in several camps, saying that in four of the region's seven refugee camps nutrition services have been suspended, endangering nearly 80,000 children under the age of five who risk severe, potentially fatal acute malnutrition, and that generalised budget cuts have plunged tens of thousands of children into a high-risk situation ; reported that since October 2024 refugees in the Kule camp have received on average only 600 calories per day, less than 30% of the recommended minimum of 2,100 calories per person per day, that other camps face similar difficulties with prolonged interruptions in food distribution due to international supply chain disruptions and lack of funding, and that in 2025 it recorded a 55% increase in admissions of children to its therapeutic nutrition centre compared with the previous year, half of them from camps other than Kule.

a1743.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) (statement/communique)
a1743.speech: Appealed: "We call on humanitarian organisations and the Ethiopian authorities to urgently step up their support and to strengthen the local health system."

a1743.speaker: Nyauahial Puoch, mother from the Tierkidi refugee camp
a1743.speech: "We receive food once a month - maize, wheat, sorghum - but it is never enough to last until the end of the month" ; "Since last year, the situation has deteriorated a great deal. Some products we used to receive are no longer provided at all."

a1765.speaker: Benjamin Kalu, Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives and co-chairman of the National Assembly constitutional review panel
a1765.speech: Revealed a fortnight ago during a plenary session of the House that the proposals for the creation of 31 new states had been sent to the House of Representatives' Joint-Committee on Constitutional Review, and further stated that the advocates of the proposals had been given up to 5 March to meet the constitutional requirements necessary for action to be taken.

a1765.speaker: Afenifere (Yoruba socio-cultural group) and the Arewa Consultative Forum
a1765.speech: Have scoffed at the idea of creating 31 new states.

a1765.speaker: Middle Belt Forum and Pan-Niger Delta Forum
a1765.speech: Are upbeat about it, provided that all the regions of the country have an equal number of states.

a1765.speaker: Ohaneze Ndigbo
a1765.speech: Questioned the distribution of the intended states, which marginalises the South-East further.

a1765.speaker: Constitution of Nigeria, Section 8 (document cited)
a1765.speech: Provides the guidelines to be met for the National Assembly's approval of any such request: first, the request must be "supported by at least two-thirds majority of members (representing the area demanding the creation of the State) in each of the following, namely," the Senate and House of Representatives; the House of Assembly in respect of the area and local government areas also. More hurdles outlined are in the conduct of a referendum with at least two-thirds of the people in support; which will further be passed in the state assembly with a two-thirds majority.

a1765.speaker: Alex Ekwueme, former Vice-President of Nigeria
a1765.speech: Put forward the six geopolitical structure at the 1995 Political Conference of the Sani Abacha regime, in an effort at restructuring the polity.

a1765.speaker: Political Conference of the Goodluck Jonathan administration (2014 conference report)
a1765.speech: Proposed 18 new states, with an additional one to the South-East to address its concern about inequity. But the conference report was neither acted on by President Jonathan, nor by President Muhammadu Buhari, subsequently.

a1765.speaker: National Bureau of Statistics, 2023 report on internally generated revenue (IGR) of the 36 states
a1765.speech: Puts this issue in sharp relief: while Lagos State generated N815.36 billion, Rivers State made N195.41 billion and Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja, N211.10 billion, to top the ranks. And, the N11.74 billion; N10.87 billion; and N11.19 billion of Kebbi, Yobe and Taraba states respectively, showed the worst indices.

a1765.speaker: Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC)
a1765.speech: Has given the affected states a March deadline to implement the new N70,000 minimum wage, or face the consequences of labour unrest.

a2339.speaker: Annika Jayawardenar, Head of Development Cooperation at the Swedish Embassy
a2339.speech: "protecting the rights of girls is key to sustaining social and economic development so learning how to uphold rights is vital," she said as she signed a Grant Agreement with Kebour Ghenna, Executive Director of IA, last Thursday.

a2339.speaker: Kebour Ghenna, Executive Director of Initiative Africa (IA)
a2339.speech: Pointed out that empowerment projects such as this one are geared towards helping young girls and women have a voice in the society and achieve their full potential ; appreciated the Swedish Embassy for the support it lent to the organization since 2006.

a2477.speaker: Salamatu Madaki, nutrition coordinator, Awe local government, Nasarawa State
a2477.speech: "We feed our children three times a day, but it's just carbohydrates. No vegetables, no beans, no meat. Mostly pap in the morning, yams in the afternoon, fufu at night."

a2477.speaker: Salamatu Madaki, nutrition coordinator, Awe local government, Nasarawa State
a2477.speech: According to Ms Madaki, between December 2024 and May 2025, cases of severe acute malnutrition in Awe jumped from 64 to 86, and moderate cases also increased, from 28 to 32.

a2477.speaker: Salamatu Madaki, nutrition coordinator, Awe local government, Nasarawa State
a2477.speech: According to Ms Madaki, the last significant support the Awe LGA received was in 2023, through the ANRIN project.

a2477.speaker: UNICEF
a2477.speech: According to UNICEF, Nigeria has the world's second-highest number of stunted children, with 32 per cent of children under five affected; about two million Nigerian children suffer from severe acute malnutrition (SAM), but only two in 10 receive treatment; seven per cent of women of childbearing age also suffer from acute malnutrition ; every hour, nearly 100 Nigerian children under five die from malnutrition or related illnesses.

a2477.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a2477.speech: Said 51.9 per cent of children in Kano are stunted due to malnutrition.

a2477.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF)
a2477.speech: Said over 650 children have died from severe acute malnutrition in Katsina State this year; the organisation, which has been operating in Katsina since 2021, said it recorded an alarming rise in the number of malnourished children brought to its treatment centres in increasingly critical condition ; said it recorded a 74.1 per cent increase in the admission of malnourished children into its facilities in Kebbi between January and June 2025.

a2477.speaker: Najahatu Salihu, mother of two in Awe
a2477.speech: "I manage a public tap and get about N500 a day from my brother-in-law. My husband works in the market. There's no way we can afford meat or milk."

a2477.speaker: Hadiza Abdullahi, 38, mother in Awe
a2477.speech: "We used to buy beans and eggs, but now we eat only rice or maize. We cook once at night and reheat it in the morning. It's the same thing every day."

a2477.speaker: Mariam Abdulhadi, grain seller in Maikunkele
a2477.speech: "She only pinches rice when I eat. She vomits most solid foods and lives mostly on breast milk." ; "One egg is now N250/N300, and fish is also expensive. She is not my only child; business has been bad these days."

a2477.speaker: Husband of Mariam Abdulhadi (recalled by her)
a2477.speech: "So she wants to enjoy when there is no money?" Mrs Abdulhadi remembers her husband saying, dismissing a health worker's suggestion of adding eggs and fish to the child's diet.

a2477.speaker: Mercy Madumbi, local nutrition officer in Maikunkele
a2477.speech: Said the state nutrition office occasionally sends supplies, but they rarely meet local needs: "Most women are unemployed. Even when food is available, they can't afford it, and they don't know how to combine what they have for better nutrition."

a2477.speaker: Mercy Madumbi, local nutrition officer in Maikunkele
a2477.speech: "Malnutrition doesn't just stunt the body. It stunts the mind, the immune system, the future."

a2477.speaker: Yakubu Maaji, ward focal person for Maikunkele
a2477.speech: Warns that rising food prices are affecting children and pregnant women: "Some babies are born malnourished because their mothers were not well-fed during pregnancy. It's transferred from mother to child" ; said that three years ago 98 per cent of children in the community were well nourished, a figure that has now dropped to 60 per cent, leaving 40 per cent malnourished.

a2477.speaker: Yakubu Maaji, ward focal person for Maikunkele
a2477.speech: "During that period, even getting water to drink or bathe is hard. We only manage to plant during the rainy season," on how a poor water supply in the dry season makes home gardening nearly impossible.

a2477.speaker: Asmau Muhammad, Niger State Nutrition Officer
a2477.speech: Said that as of 2024, Niger State recorded 3,570 reported cases of malnutrition among children under five; called for urgent government and donor funding, expansion of the Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) programme, and the upgrade of primary healthcare centres with solar power, clean water, and essential supplies like MUAC tapes and Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF); also stressed the need to engage traditional leaders, promote peer support groups, and use local-language radio to improve awareness of exclusive breastfeeding and proper child feeding.

a2477.speaker: Marylyne Malomba, nutrition consultant for the International Medical Corps
a2477.speech: "If the mother has not stocked up enough nutrients, then the child will not get enough. Limbs, organs, and even brain development are affected by a lack of nutrients when the child is still a fetus" ; "So it's important to understand that the health of the mother at the point of pregnancy is one of the most important places to start taking care of the child."

a2477.speaker: Hasanna Isah, mother in Maikunkele
a2477.speech: "He was born weak and underweight, not in a hospital" ; "One sachet is N200 and I can stretch it for two feedings. But it's not every time I have the money" ; "We eat tuwo with dry okra or baobab soup. Meat is out of reach. I sometimes buy N100 fried fish-gangaria, and shred it so it can go round" ; "One bunch is N200, and it's not enough for my children. Sometimes that's all the money I have."

a2477.speaker: National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)
a2477.speech: Headline inflation peaked at 34.8 per cent in December 2024 before the National Bureau of Statistics rebased its Consumer Price Index; the new basket lowered the figure to 24.48 per cent in January, and by June the country's annual inflation stood at 22.22 per cent, with food inflation reaching 21.97 per cent year-on-year.

a2477.speaker: President Bola Tinubu
a2477.speech: In July 2023, declared a state of emergency regarding food insecurity.

a2477.speaker: SBM Jollof Index / report "Staple Under Stress"
a2477.speech: According to the SBM Jollof Index, the cost of cooking a pot of jollof rice rose 19 per cent between September 2024 and March 2025, from N21,300 to N25,486; the report attributed the rise to soaring prices of ingredients like pepper, onions, rice, turkey, and beef.

a2477.speaker: 2024 Global Hunger Index
a2477.speech: Nigeria is ranked 110th out of 127 countries with enough data to calculate the scores; with a score of 28.8, Nigeria faces a serious level of hunger.

a2477.speaker: The Economist Intelligence Unit (2022 Global Food Security Index)
a2477.speech: Noted that Nigeria scored 0.0 on policy commitments for food security and access, compared to a global average of 47.1, with Nigeria ranked 107th out of 113 countries and 25th out of 28 in Sub-Saharan Africa.

a2477.speaker: Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS)
a2477.speech: Shows that child nutrition has worsened in the past five years: in 2018, 37 per cent of children under five were stunted; by 2023, it rose to 40 per cent; underweight cases climbed from 22 to 27 per cent, while wasting increased from 7 to 8 per cent.

a2477.speaker: Civil Society Scaling Up Nutrition in Nigeria (CS-SUNN)
a2477.speech: Said these figures show a worsening trend even in states with minor changes, and that population growth has masked any real improvement; continues to advocate for stronger policies, improved budget releases, and better access to RUTF, and has also pushed for a six-month paid maternity leave bill and the completion of Nigeria's revised nutrition policy.

a2477.speaker: International Rescue Committee (IRC)
a2477.speech: Recently raised alarm over the growing number of severely malnourished children in its clinics across Northern Nigeria, with the crisis expected to worsen during the lean season, as insecurity, aid cuts, climate shocks, and severe flooding deepen food scarcity.

a2477.speaker: Babatunde Ojei, Country Director, IRC Nigeria
a2477.speech: "Children are especially vulnerable during this period. It's heartbreaking to see the needs growing while support shrinks. Violence and insecurity are cutting off communities, leaving children without the care they desperately need."

a2477.speaker: Munachisom Favour, vegetable seller in Gosa Market, Abuja
a2477.speech: "We eat without meat or fish. I can't afford to give my children what they need."

a2477.speaker: Paul Alaje, senior economist at SPM Professionals
a2477.speech: Argues that inflation is a major factor driving malnutrition in Nigeria because the rising cost of food has placed basic nutrition out of reach for many households; noted that more than 40 per cent of the population lives on very low or fixed incomes, making it difficult for them to afford the foods necessary for healthy living; said no amount of medication or nutritional supplements can adequately address malnutrition without access to actual food; explained that unless inflation drops to single digits and people have more purchasing power, families will continue to struggle with food insecurity: "Inflation is one of the major contributors to household malnutrition. Food costs have become unreachable for low-income families, who comprise over 40 per cent of our population. Nutrition cannot rely on supplements alone. Without access to real food, families will continue to suffer."

a2812.speaker: National Institute for Disaster Risk Management (INGD) of Mozambique
a2812.speech: The situation is considered dramatic and is worrying the National Institute for Disaster Risk Management, which suggests greater internal solidarity; the Institute continues to provide assistance to vulnerable populations, but with limitations due to the reduction in international humanitarian aid.

a2812.speaker: Official statistics
a2812.speech: According to official statistics, Cabo Delgado has around 500,000 people living as displaced persons, mostly because of the terrorist attacks.

a2989.speaker: 2018 Labour Force Survey
a2989.speech: Namibia's agriculture sector is largely based on primary production representing the largest employer in the country, accounting for about 23% of the total labour force (2018 Labour Force Survey).

a2989.speaker: Economists
a2989.speech: Economists are projecting a devastating impact on health, economic performance, poverty, unemployment, low investments and high public debts as a result of Covid-19.

a3318.speaker: Tundu Lissu, CHADEMA leader
a3318.speech: Is on trial for treason, charges he denies.

a3318.speaker: Amnesty International (statement of October 20)
a3318.speech: Accused the authorities of repressing dissent, charges the government denied ; “Authorities must end their unacceptable campaign of repression against dissent,” Amnesty said in its statement on October 20 ; the rights watchdog said it had in fact asked authorities to respond before publishing the statement.

a3318.speaker: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), U.S. crisis-monitoring group
a3318.speech: Said CCM was intent on maintaining its status as the “last hegemonic liberation party in southern Africa” and avoiding the recent electoral pressures faced by counterparts in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe.

a3318.speaker: Tanzania electoral commission
a3318.speech: Says it will announce the results within three days of election day.

a3318.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a3318.speech: Has boasted about expanding road and railway networks and increasing power generation capacity; in her next term, she has promised to prioritise hiring more teachers ; has said her government is committed to respecting human rights and last year ordered an investigation into the reports of abductions.

a3318.speaker: Rights campaigners and opposition candidates
a3318.speech: Have accused the government of unexplained abductions of its critics.

a3318.speaker: Family of the former Tanzanian ambassador to Cuba
a3318.speech: Said he was taken from his home by unknown assailants.

a3318.speaker: Gerson Msigwa, Tanzanian government spokesperson
a3318.speech: Said Amnesty had not asked authorities to respond before publishing the statement ; “The brief’s portrayal of Tanzania as a country that tolerates arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and suppression of freedoms is inconsistent with the legal and institutional safeguards in place,” Msigwa said in a statement.

a3447.speaker: U.S. Supreme Court (ruling of March 5, 2025)
a3447.speech: Ordered the Trump administration to resume disbursement of frozen international aid estimated at between 1.5 and 2 billion dollars, by a 5-4 vote; reinstated the payment order and sent the matter back to the original judge to set a new "realistic" deadline for its execution, the February 27 date having passed.

a3447.speaker: Federal judge (petitioned by NGOs and beneficiary companies)
a3447.speech: Suspended the 90-day aid freeze, holding that it exceeded presidential prerogatives over funds approved by Congress, and set February 27 as the date for payments to resume.

a3447.speaker: Justice Samuel Alito, writing for the four dissenting conservative Supreme Court justices (Alito, Thomas, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh)
a3447.speech: "The Court makes an extremely regrettable misstep by rewarding judicial overreach and imposing a 2-billion-dollar penalty on American taxpayers." While acknowledging the plaintiffs' "serious concerns" about payment for work already performed, he judged the solution "too extreme."

a3447.speaker: Trump administration (announcement of February 26)
a3447.speech: Announced the elimination of 92% of USAID's foreign funding, representing nearly 60 billion dollars in savings promised to taxpayers.

a3447.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President (executive order of January 20, 2025)
a3447.speech: By executive order ordered a 90-day freeze on U.S. foreign aid, with the aim of reviewing programs funded by USAID.

a3655.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a3655.speech: "The specter of thirst is tangible in Djibouti," ; revealed that the solution to this problem at home consisted in "putting in place a policy of settling nomadic populations around water points, through, among other things, the mobilization of groundwater and runoff water and boreholes" ; said the Horn of Africa risks "becoming uninhabitable in the coming decades, because of heat waves that should exceed the physiological and social limits of man" ; "The Horn of Africa will be among the most affected, with forecasts of an increase of 2.7 to 3.6 C in the years to come" ; "With hydroelectricity imported from Ethiopia and a wind farm that produces 60 megawatts, we have today reached 80% energy mix. We are also exploring our solar and geothermal potential, which are formidable." ; "We created in October 2022 a Regional Research Observatory for the Environment and the Climate"

a3655.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti
a3655.speech: Deplored the delays in the implementation of "mechanisms dedicated to global warming and above all despite the numerous commitments made by industrialized countries" ; "It is not fair that we leave every conference with a taste of unfinished business," urging the international community to address climate challenges more collegially ; "It is urgent that we act collectively before the opportunities for action are lost and before it is too late," calling for greater subscription by the world's nations to the "reduction of greenhouse gases, the management of loss and damage, the mobilization of resources" and to development practices more based on the "protection of the environment" ; "The legal and legitimate choice would be to develop while protecting the environment together, because living in harmony implies balance and equity." ; "We Africans are among the most impacted even though our contribution is less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions." ; "Unfortunately, we are obliged to go into debt to finance these green projects and to adapt... We are not asking for a special favor but for a just and equitable approach to the fight against global warming."

a3673.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a3673.speech: Documented over 1,180 confirmed deaths during Sahara crossings between 2020 and May 2024, a figure widely accepted as a severe underestimation, given the desert’s vast, lawless expanses.

a3673.speaker: Nigerian Immigration Service
a3673.speech: Disclosed in 2017 that over 10,000 Nigerians perished in a mere five-month span while attempting to flee; nearly half drowned in the Mediterranean, the rest succumbed to the desert.

a3673.speaker: Warsan Shire, Somali-British poet
a3673.speech: “No one leaves home unless home is the mouth of a shark.”

a3824.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a3824.speech: The UN agency said it suspended malnutrition treatment for 650,000 malnourished women and children in Ethiopia this week due to severe funding shortages, with millions more at risk of losing access to aid ; according to WFP, more than 10-million people in Ethiopia are gravely short of food, including 3-million displaced by conflict and extreme weather conditions as well as refugees from war-torn neighbouring Sudan ; WFP previously warned of a return of drought conditions to the region this year.

a3824.speaker: Zlatan Milisic, WFP country director in Ethiopia
a3824.speech: Said WFP gets financing from 15-20 donors including the US but many of them have cut funding this year ; added that the agency has received exemptions from US President Donald Trump’s aid freeze that has disrupted humanitarian work around the world, but little for 2025 so far ; said WFP had already reduced rations in recent months but that its operations were now at “breaking point” due to severe underfunding, forcing more drastic measures ; “We’ve been left no choice but to this week suspend treatment for 650,000 malnourished women and children — simply because we’ve run out of commodities and funding,” he told a Geneva press briefing by video from Addis Ababa ; added that around 3.6-million people could lose access to assistance, including some being treated for malnutrition, if more funding is not received by June ; “I would hope that we will get the resources and put in place measures to really do our best to assist them. But if they don’t receive assistance, we will have serious consequences.”

a3824.speaker: WFP spokesperson
a3824.speech: Later added that those cut off were in various locations including the northern regions of Tigray and Afar, and that the UN agency is actively seeking funding to purchase more supplies to resume treatments.

a4180.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a4180.speech: has said that Sub-Saharan Africa's economic growth has continued to be dragged down by underperformance in its three largest economies, namely Nigeria, South Africa, and Angola ; stated that Sub-Saharan Africa's economic growth is being weighed down by sluggish performances in the continent's biggest economies ; noted that, excluding Nigeria, South Africa, and Angola, the rest of the region is projected to grow by 4.6% in 2025 and a robust 5.7% in the subsequent years ; “Despite a slight rebound in regional growth, the largest economies are not pulling their weight.” ; “This is constraining the region's full potential at a time when many smaller economies are showing strong momentum.”

a4180.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a4180.speech: According to the report, in 2024, about 70% of Sub-Saharan African countries saw inflation decline due to improved currency stability, tighter monetary and fiscal policies, and easing global supply chain pressures. However, inflation remains high in several countries, noting that 14 out of 47 nations still report double-digit inflation, including Nigeria, Angola, Ghana, Malawi, Sudan, and Zimbabwe.

a4180.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a4180.speech: stated that many governments across Sub-Saharan Africa struggle to balance rising debt service costs with investment needs in critical infrastructure and social sectors.

a4180.speaker: World Bank (Africa's Pulse report)
a4180.speech: “Growth prospects in the region are held back by the inadequacy of preventive and coping strategies to address conflict and climate change. The incidence and severity of conflict and violence across areas of the subcontinent increased throughout 2024 and the start of this year. In 2024, fatalities caused by the Islamist insurgency remained at an all-time high, with the Sahel accounting for more than half of the Islamist activity on the subcontinent. The rise in conflict has led to acute food insecurity and a rapid increase in food emergencies. Recent estimations suggest that around 120 million Africans face acute food insecurity, of which 80 percent live in countries experiencing conflict. This situation will be compounded by reduced official development assistance for emergency response. Rising temperatures, anomalous rainfall patterns, and multiyear extreme weather events are repeatedly battering Sub-Saharan African countries.”

a4180.speaker: World Bank
a4180.speech: warned that without significant improvements in governance, conflict resolution, and climate resilience strategies, many countries in Sub-Saharan Africa may struggle to sustain meaningful economic progress despite the global recovery.

a4183.speaker: Aide Memoire (agreement signed by MCC and the Government of Mozambique)
a4183.speech: This non-binding document details the two governments' agreement on the scope and objectives of MCC's compact with Mozambique. The priorities include 1) Connectivity and rural transport, 2) Promotion of investment in commercial agriculture, and 3) Integrated climate management and coastal development. Under the Aide Memoire, the Government of Mozambique has committed to increase its allocation of funding to Mozambique's road maintenance system under the Administração Nacional de Estradas and Fundo de Estradas by 50 percent, or USD $37.5 million.

a4183.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) and the Mozambican Government
a4183.speech: expect to sign the proposed compact in 2023.

a4254.speaker: Bush-era report
a4254.speech: Suggests that anthropogenic climate change is only one “narrative” among others.

a4254.speaker: Big Oil
a4254.speech: Begins talking about historical carbon emissions and telling us that developing nations must be allowed to industrialise.

a4254.speaker: Rob Nixon, author of “Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor”
a4254.speech: Addresses the challenge of giving dramatic visibility to the complex politics and “attritional lethality” of environmental crises; levels against American environmentalism the charge that it has remained scandalously parochial, obsessed with images of the West while remaining almost entirely un-engaged with the long-term consequences of American foreign policy — the “offshore histories” of nuclear testing in the Pacific, Agent Orange in Vietnam, depleted uranium in Iraq ; asks how writers can plot and give figurative shape to “formless threats whose fatal repercussions are dispersed across space and time”, the “long dyings” and “disasters that are anonymous and star nobody”, and to “calamities that patiently dispense their devastation while remaining outside our flickering attention spans – and outside the purview of a spectacle driven corporate media”; asks what chances there are for digital activism when the electronic screen has itself become “an ecosystem of interruption technologies”.

a4254.speaker: Rob Nixon, author of “Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor”
a4254.speech: Suggests that Arundhati Roy's prime contribution as a writer-activist was “to expose the insidious, traumatic violence inflicted on the most vulnerable, human and nonhuman, by the affectless language of technospeak”, the personal essay as a “small, nimble form” having “allowed her to take on the weighty, leaden genres that gave ballast to the culture of the megadam and, beyond that, to the culture of developmental gigantism”.

a4254.speaker: Rob Nixon, author of “Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor”
a4254.speech: Argues that South Africa is a site where “the segregations of humans from non-humans have long been implicated in the violent segregations of humans from humans”, that across much of Southern and East Africa “game” reserves and “native” reserves “have shadowed each other historically in the interdependent administrations of conservation, leisure and labour”, and reads the contemporary South African game reserve as a paradoxical space risking becoming a site where “a provincial whiteness is fortified by white pilgrims from abroad”.

a4254.speaker: Lawrence Summers, then Chief Economist of the World Bank (leaked memo of 12 December 1991)
a4254.speech: “I think the economic logic behind dumping a load of toxic waste in the lowest wage country is impeccable and we should face up to that... I've always thought that under-populated countries in Africa are vastly UNDER-polluted, their air quality is probably vastly inefficiently low compared to Los Angeles or Mexico City... Just between you and me, shouldn't the World Bank be encouraging MORE migration of the dirty industries to the LDCs [Least Developed Countries]?”

a4254.speaker: Arundhati Roy, writer-activist (“Power Politics”, 2001)
a4254.speech: Writes of visiting a conference on water privatisation: “Language is the skin of my thought… At the Hague I stumbled on a denomination, a sub-world, whose life's endeavour was the opposite of mine.
