For them the whole purpose of language is to mask intent… They breed and prosper in the space that lies between what they say and what they sell.”

a4254.speaker: Arundhati Roy, writer-activist
a4254.speech: “…Let's pick our parts, put on these discarded costumes and speak our second-hand lines in this sad second-hand play. But let's not forget that the stakes we're playing for are huge. Our fatigue and our shame could mean the end of us.”

a4327.speaker: Abdu Mukhtar, National Coordinator, Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC)
a4327.speech: Said during an appearance on the Your Voice podcast that the initiative aims to increase local drug production from 20 per cent to 80 per cent by 2030: “If you look at the current situation in Nigeria, we import about 80 per cent of the medical drugs and therapeutics, about 100 per cent of the vaccines, and about 99 per cent of the medical devices, including test kits that we use in this country,” ; “So what the presidential initiative is supposed to address is to be able to reverse those numbers.”

a4327.speaker: Abdu Mukhtar, National Coordinator, Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC)
a4327.speech: Explained that the initiative’s goals include increasing local production of medical drugs, reducing outbound medical tourism and creating jobs: “We spend almost $2 billion every year on our citizens going abroad to receive healthcare in different parts of the world, including some African countries, in Asia, US and so on. So the second mandate is to reduce that,” ; “Then the third one is to create jobs across the various parts of the healthcare value chain. You know, the healthcare value chain is very extensive, you can create value everywhere, but the value should be translated into jobs.” ; said the government will strengthen regulatory institutions like NAFDAC and establish new research and development capabilities, and reduce medical tourism by building specialised hospitals and diagnostic facilities and training specialised doctors and nurses.

a4327.speaker: Abdu Mukhtar, National Coordinator, Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC)
a4327.speech: Emphasised that the initiative aims to make Nigeria a leader in vaccine development and production, with Nigerian-made drugs, vaccines and devices available locally and across West Africa, Africa and globally; spoke on the benefits of the executive order removing VAT on imported equipment and raw materials; and emphasised strategic partnerships across the private and public sectors, institutions, stakeholders and donors, adding that Nigeria needs to harness the power of the Nigerian diaspora.

a4327.speaker: Mojisola Adeyeye, Director General, National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
a4327.speech: Said the country’s dependence on foreign products rather than locally manufactured ones significantly contributes to these challenges; speaking in May at a webinar organised by The Cable Newspaper, pointed out that the quantity of locally manufactured drugs remains lower compared to those produced by foreign pharmaceutical companies and imported into the country, added that all the items used for manufacturing drugs locally are also imported, and said this has contributed significantly to drug insecurity and restricted access to medication and medical care caused by an over-inflated cost.

a4351.speaker: Partnership agreement between Citrus International Trading Plc and Butyl Products Ltd
a4351.speech: According to the partnership agreement that Citrus sealed with Butyl Products Ltd, they will begin introducing new tanker products and accessories used for emergency relief, housing projects and other mega projects at their site.

a4351.speaker: Citrus International Trading Plc
a4351.speech: Stated that supplying Butyl's product would be a good opportunity to expand safe water throughout Ethiopia.

a4351.speaker: Craig Ball, Sales Director of Butyl Products Ltd
a4351.speech: Stated they are the biggest tanker supplier in the world for aid agencies ; said that his company has agreed with Citrus because they are trusted by international and local aid agencies as they have been supplying water purification tablets for the last decade ; "We are not new to the Ethiopian market but the deal with citrus will create a better," Ball told Capital ; added that the prices of his products are comparable to similar overseas companies.

a4351.speaker: Craig Ball, Sales Director of Butyl Products Ltd
a4351.speech: Stated that his company has installed a product called Flexigester V80 at the project in the Wukro, Tigray region carried out under a local NGO called Elshadai Orphanage ; said that Flexigester V80, which is one of several products Butyl makes, is an innovative anaerobic digestion system that can take materials such as animal manure, unused food, human waste and plants and convert them, over a period of several weeks, into natural bio-fertilizer and biogas.

a4351.speaker: Menassie Kifle, GM of Citrus
a4351.speech: Said that the water tanker product is already installed for a hotel facility at Afar recently ; added that in the coming week the tanker will be erected at the site of Ethiopian Airlines employees' housing project at Ayat area ; "Some companies and organizations have already shown their interest to use the product since it is more durable, easily installed within very few weeks and cost wise than concrete tanker."

a4419.speaker: Organisers of the Beginnings Fund (statement)
a4419.speech: Said the US$500-million fund set a deadline of 2030 to reach its target and has already reached US$450 million in pledges; said the fund seeks to prevent more than 300 000 deaths and improve access to quality care for 34 million mothers and babies by that date.

a4419.speaker: Beginnings Fund statement
a4419.speech: Said most deaths in sub-Saharan Africa occur within the first month of life, and the region accounts for 70% of global maternal deaths, with 182 000 women and 1.2 million newborns dying each year from preventable causes, along with 950 000 stillbirths.

a4419.speaker: Tala Al Ramahi, spokeswoman for the Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity
a4419.speech: “It’s a very critical time,” she said of the aid freeze ordered by United States president Donald Trump, which has slashed budgets for many humanitarian programmes ; “Philanthropy cannot fill the gaps that the aid cuts have left behind,” she told AFP, but the Beginnings Fund will target “the products, people, and systems required to improve and scale maternal and neonatal health”.

a4419.speaker: The United Arab Emirates (Emirates government)
a4419.speech: Denies any military involvement in the conflicts in Sudan and Libya despite evidence presented by the United Nations and many other agencies.

a4752.speaker: Report by the Prioritising SPS Investment for Market Access (P-IMA) tool
a4752.speech: Outlined that the investment need for groundnut would generate a possible value change of $5.7 million for The Gambia ; lists cashew nuts tagged at $3,478,000 with a value change of $52,359,000 as the first priority, followed by groundnut, which requires aflatoxin control and management with an investment need of $573,500 to obtain a value change of $5,700,000.

a4752.speaker: Abdoulie Jallow, member of the technical team and senior staff member of the Food Safety and Quality Authority (FSQA)
a4752.speech: Said if the country focused on the identified issues of its export products, it would generate more income and its farmers would have more money.

a4752.speaker: Momomdou Bah, director of the Food Safety and Quality Authority (FSQA)
a4752.speech: Said groundnut used to be one of Gambia’s major export commodities in the international market, but recently, with the high availability of aflatoxin, Gambian groundnuts are no longer exported to European markets.

a4818.speaker: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) website
a4818.speech: Indicated that the United Nations has allocated 110 million dollars to provide assistance in ten crisis situations in Africa, Asia and Latin America; a third of that sum will go to help Sudan, beset by violence, forced displacement and famine, as well as refugees in Chad, with humanitarian aid for African countries also going to the Central African Republic, Mauritania, Niger, Somalia and Zambia, and funds also financing initiatives to save lives and protect vulnerable people from climate disasters.

a4818.speaker: Tom Fletcher, UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator
a4818.speech: “For countries affected by conflict, climate change and economic upheaval, drastic funding cuts do not mean that humanitarian needs will disappear. The emergency funds allocated today make it possible to rapidly channel resources to where they are most needed.”

a4985.speaker: Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey in Benin (MICS 2021-2022) report
a4985.speech: The report sets out the major advances and the challenges ahead, giving Benin reliable and up-to-date indicators for monitoring progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, and highlighting progress and challenges in fertility, family planning, child mortality, maternal and child health, children's nutritional status, early childhood development, protection of children and women, water quality, the impacts of Covid-19 and information and communication technologies.

a4985.speaker: Aude Rogot, deputy representative of UNICEF
a4985.speech: commends Benin for its major advances: "I salute here the progress achieved by Benin on certain indicators where an overall improvement is observed between 2014 and 2021-2022, notably under-five mortality, which fell from 115 per thousand to 80 per thousand, the net primary school admission rate (52% to about 62%), birth registration (85% to 93%), child labour (53% to 20%), early marriage (32% to 28%)" ; she also examines attitudes towards domestic violence among women (36% to 29%), the use of improved drinking water sources (72% to 77%), the existence of a handwashing facility with water and soap (8% to 12%), and the use of improved toilets (13% to 41%).

a4985.speaker: Aude Rogot, deputy representative of UNICEF
a4985.speech: remains unsatisfied regarding full vaccination coverage, which fell from "41.6% in 2014 to 27.6% in 2021-2022, underweight prevalence, which rose from 18% in 2014 to 21% in 2021-2022; stunting from 34% to 36.5% and wasting from 4.5% to 8.3% over the same period".

a4985.speaker: Laurent Hounsa, director general of the National Institute of Statistics and Demography (InStaD)
a4985.speech: explains: "This second edition of the MICS survey comes at a time when the government and its partners need, more than ever, recent, detailed and disaggregated demographic data in order to take better account of population parameters, and specifically the vulnerable groups that are women and children, in economic and social development policies."

a5030.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of Somalia
a5030.speech: Led the national ceremony in Mogadishu, where he paid tribute to the country’s founding leaders, freedom fighters, and the spirit of unity that brought together the northern and southern regions on July 1, 1960 ; in his address, the president called for national cohesion, dialogue, and sustained commitment to federalism and reconciliation.

a5030.speaker: Italian Embassy in Mogadishu (statement posted on social media)
a5030.speech: Conveyed its congratulations, stating: “On the occasion of Somali Independence Day, Italy in Somalia extends heartfelt wishes for a prosperous future to the Somali people.”

a5030.speaker: King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden
a5030.speech: Delivered a message to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, expressing warm congratulations and best wishes to the government and people of Somalia; the message, shared via national media, reflected Sweden’s ongoing support for Somalia’s state-building efforts.

a5030.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Mogadishu (statement)
a5030.speech: Published a statement noting: “The United States congratulates the people of Somalia on their Independence Day.”

a5030.speaker: British Embassy in Somalia (message on behalf of King Charles III)
a5030.speech: Released a message on behalf of King Charles III, offering warm wishes to the Somali people as they celebrated 65 years of independence.

a5030.speaker: Moussa Faki Mahamat, Chairperson of the African Union Commission
a5030.speech: Extended formal congratulations to the people and government of Somalia; the AU praised the resilience of the Somali people and reaffirmed its steadfast support for Somalia’s national priorities.

a5030.speaker: Acting head of the African Union’s peace support mission in Somalia (ATMIS)
a5030.speech: In a separate statement, commended Somali security forces for their contributions to peace and stability.

a5242.speaker: Joel Akowanou, Director of Operations of MCA-Benin II
a5242.speech: "We are therefore in a transition towards an intelligent system where we can intervene very quickly on the network and control consumption, production..."

a5242.speaker: Gerard Zagrodnik, Director General of the Beninese Electric Energy Company (SBEE); Brian Shukan, US Ambassador to Benin; Alice Albright, CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC); and Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State in charge of Development and Coordination of Government Action and chairman of the board of MCA-Benin II
a5242.speech: each in turn welcomed the fact that this infrastructure is a first in Benin.

a5242.speaker: Gerard Zagrodnik, Director General of the Beninese Electric Energy Company (SBEE)
a5242.speech: presented to the audience the mission of the centre and its advantages for Benin in energy and economic terms: "The mission of the centre is to ensure the balance between production and consumption at the lowest cost, under optimal conditions of security and quality (...). This centre has extremely important responsibilities, in particular the steering, monitoring and remote control of installations, the management of supply and demand (...). It therefore plays a leading role in the use of the investments that have been made over the past few years. With its capacity for modelling and simulating the network, this centre will also make it possible to optimise future investments, to run simulations before investing, to evaluate, to find options..."

a5242.speaker: Brian Shukan, US Ambassador to Benin
a5242.speech: "we could also call it the command and control centre of Benin's electricity network. In this operations centre, which works 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (...), operators are trained to identify and resolve the faults of the Beninese electricity network..."

a5242.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State in charge of Development and Coordination of Government Action
a5242.speech: "It is a centre that will allow us to better manage the distribution of energy in our country and to substantially reduce the duration of outages/load-shedding..." ; on behalf of the government, the Minister of State renewed Benin's commitment to sustaining all the gains so that everyone, without distinction, has access to reliable, quality electricity at the lowest cost, for the country's socio-economic development.

a5307.speaker: John Grabowski, regional advisor for USAID
a5307.speech: Said that the USA would continue to support Mozambicans and work to reduce the suffering of those displaced: "Much depends on the Mozambican government, but the US government and the American people are always ready to advance humanitarian assistance."

a5307.speaker: One displaced woman (anonymous, told DW Africa)
a5307.speech: "I left Macomia to flee the war, because there was nowhere to stay and nothing to eat. I came here with my seven children to Pemba, to my brother-in-law's house."

a5307.speaker: Local USAID representative (John Grabowski)
a5307.speech: "We thought about ways to support displaced families' livelihood, so that they have a certain income."

a5307.speaker: Experts from the Institute for Security Studies
a5307.speech: Called for urgent intervention by the African Union and the Southern African Development Community on the Cabo Delgado issue.

a5307.speaker: SADC heads of state
a5307.speech: Pledged to support Mozambique in the fight against terrorism.

a5307.speaker: John Grabowski, USAID advisor
a5307.speech: Warns that humanitarian organisations are finding it difficult to access some areas in the north of the province, the requisite security conditions for organisations to assist the families there being lacking: "The humanitarian community is saying that it is not safe [to work in these places], and we cannot put humanitarian aid workers' lives at risk." ; "Donors, including the United States government, are concentrating their activities mainly in the southern districts, hoping for an opening going forward to effectively reach those displaced in the northern districts, which are less secure."

a5610.speaker: Financial experts (speaking at the 27th African Securities Exchanges Association conference)
a5610.speech: have argued that Africa needs to develop vibrant capital markets to bolster its economic growth and accelerate sustainable development; noted that Africa can benefit from viable capital markets through the mobilisation of its domestic resources at a time the continent is facing high indebtedness and lack of affordable finance.

a5610.speaker: Jean-Marc Kilolo, Economic Affairs Officer with the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a5610.speech: “Access to finance is a major constraint to African development and capital markets are a key player to overcome this constraint” ; said African countries are spending more in debt repayments than the amount they are getting from concessional funding and foreign aid ; “In tackling the perceived risk in Africa, it is very important to make sure that African officials know how to engage sovereign credit rating agencies; so we need to build statistical capacity to provide accurate information so that we have assessments that reflect our potential”, emphasising that the African Peer Review Mechanism is supporting the establishment of an Africa credit rating agency to provide an alternative assessment that accounts for Africa’s idiosyncrasies ; ECA has been pushing for the reform of the global financial architecture, with the aim to reform sovereign credit rating to reduce the perceived risk of Africa and get an accurate assessment of countries’ creditworthiness.

a5610.speaker: Kopano Bolokwe, Botswana Stock Exchange chairperson
a5610.speech: said African countries need to establish and integrate their capital markets as one of the means to deal with its environmental and political risks ; highlighted the need to recognize the differences between African countries in governing laws, securities rules, trading and post-trading, clearing and settlement mechanisms in looking at market integration ; challenged African stock exchanges and brokers to do the “heavy lifting” in ensuring the smooth integration of capital markets across the continent.

a5793.speaker: Prince K. Moye, Bong County Senator (Liberia)
a5793.speech: Told journalists that rice produced from his farms will be bagged and sold for a reasonable price on the local market, and that yield from his rice farm would be placed on the market for consumption as his way of contributing towards food security of Liberia. “We as leaders need to begin taking steps in making our country food sufficient. When public officials adopt these steps, it will greatly help the agriculture sector,” Senator Moye said.

a5793.speaker: Christopher Sankolo, Director General of the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority (LACRA)
a5793.speech: Heaped praises on the lawmaker, describing him as a farsighted and development-oriented leader of Bong County, and said the lawmaker’s action is worthy of commendation particularly at a time when the government is struggling to make Liberia food secure. “Senator Moye has proven to be a national leader as demonstrated by his actions. “I would like to appreciate him for his intervention as former National Campaigning Chairman of the Unity Party. This is welcoming.” ; Said these are initiatives that demonstrate love for the country, adding "We hope that others will emulate what you are doing as we strive to make Liberia a food secure nation."

a5793.speaker: Christopher Sankolo, Director General of the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority (LACRA)
a5793.speech: Encouraged Senator Prince K. Moye to do intercropping, especially with cocoa and coffee, and encouraged Liberian farmers to get involved within the cocoa and coffee sector by investing in the sector.

a5793.speaker: 2021 Global Hunger Index (report)
a5793.speech: Classifies Liberia’s level of hunger as ‘serious.’ Liberia ranked 110 of 116 countries on hunger conditions.

a5900.speaker: Food Reserve Agency (FRA)
a5900.speech: Says it has procured about 146,948 metric tonnes as of July 25, 2023 in the ongoing marketing season.

a5900.speaker: John Chipandwe, FRA Public Relations Coordinator
a5900.speech: Says this is equivalent to 2,938,370 by 50 kilogram bags of white maize ; said the agency has paid out K595,945,280 to farmers that have so far delivered Grade ‘A’ white maize during the on-going crop-marketing season ; has noted so far that the response from farmers is encouraging and that those that have not delivered the crop should do so.

a5900.speaker: Zambia Consumer Association (ZACA)
a5900.speech: Has wondered why export of maize to countries such as Kenya and Congo has continued despite the high cost of mealie meal in Zambia.

a5900.speaker: Juba Sakala, ZACA Executive Director
a5900.speech: Says the cost of living in Zambia has continued to increase as seen in the current mealie meal prices ; says there is need for Government to offload more maize on the market to help reduce the prices of mealie meal ; says Government should prioritise the local people before making decisions to export the commodity ; says Government should also engage stakeholders to put in place deliberate measures that will help mitigate the cost of living.

a5919.speaker: Nigerien authorities / Government of Niger (announcement)
a5919.speech: Announced the establishment of a working group tasked with considering a revision of the pricing structure for hydrocarbons, with a view to lowering the price at the pump.

a5919.speaker: Minister of Petroleum of Niger (communication to the Council of Ministers of Monday 24 June)
a5919.speech: Indicated that, on the instructions of the Head of State, a working group has been established to consider revising the structure of hydrocarbon prices with a view to lowering the price at the pump.

a5919.speaker: Official Nigerien press agency
a5919.speech: Noted that this reduction in the pump price is a pressing demand of civil society organisations.

a5919.speaker: Mohamed Ben Omar, former Minister of Communication of Niger (deceased)
a5919.speech: According to explanations he gave at the time, the late President Tandja, the architect of the exploitation of Niger's oil, envisaged a price of between 300 and 400 CFA francs per litre of petrol.

a6138.speaker: Federal Supervisory Authority for Foundations (ASF), Switzerland (official publication)
a6138.speech: Published today “an appeal to creditors following the liquidation of the foundation registered in Geneva” in the Swiss Official Gazette of Commerce ; also according to the ASF, it had demanded that the GHF clarify the situation by the end of June, since it was not complying with certain legal obligations.

a6138.speaker: Federal Department of Home Affairs, Switzerland
a6138.speech: Told the news agency France-Presse (AFP) that the ASF “may order the dissolution of the foundation if no creditor comes forward within the legal deadline of 30 days.”

a6138.speaker: Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF)
a6138.speech: According to the ASF, the GHF confirmed “that it never carried out any activity in Switzerland as a foundation and that it intends to dissolve the foundation registered in Geneva.”

a6138.speaker: Around 170 international NGOs
a6138.speech: Called on Tuesday for an end to the new aid distribution system and a return to the mechanism that was in force until March, when aid distribution was coordinated by several organisations and UN agencies.

a6286.speaker: Reports (unnamed estimates cited by Baraarug)
a6286.speech: Reports estimate national prevalence of female genital mutilation (FGM) among women aged 15–49 in Somalia to be 99.2%.

a6401.speaker: African Union report (August 2024)
a6401.speech: According to the report, the four confirmed candidates for the AUC chairperson position, to take over from current chairperson Moussa Faki Mahamat, are Mahamoud Ali Youssouf of Djibouti, Raila Odinga of Kenya, Richard Randriamandrato of Madagascar and Anil Gayan of Mauritius.

a6401.speaker: Raila Odinga, veteran Kenyan opposition leader and AUC chairperson candidate
a6401.speech: "We are focused on bringing the seat home for Kenya and serving the African people," Odinga said on X while announcing his formal candidacy.

a6401.speaker: Raila Odinga, veteran Kenyan opposition leader and AUC chairperson candidate
a6401.speech: In a flagship statement posted via his social media platforms, Odinga said Museveni endorsed him during a joint meeting with President William Ruto; the Azimio alliance's leader stated that the joint meeting with President Museveni and President Ruto was organized at the Ugandan president's invitation.

a6401.speaker: Media report titled "Museveni Endorses Raila Odinga's AU Chairperson Bid" (March 2024)
a6401.speech: The report, circulated in the East African region, showed the publicity campaign and erratic steps at promoting Kenyan Raila Odinga to take over as Chairman of the AU Commission.

a6401.speaker: Mahamoud Ali Youssouf, Foreign Minister of Djibouti and AUC chairperson candidate
a6401.speech: "I am the only candidate capable of bridging the gap between the different regions of Africa, being French-speaking, but also English-speaking and Arabic-speaking" ; "My primary objective if I am elected is to silence the guns" on the continent, he told AFP in an interview in July ; believes that although Djibouti is a small country with a sizable port, his government hopes to develop its economy along the same lines as Dubai.

a6401.speaker: Mahamoud Ali Youssouf's biography
a6401.speech: His biography says that between 1985 and 1990 he studied foreign languages at the Lumiere University Lyon, then studied business management at the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom, and was unsuccessful with his thesis at the Universite libre de Bruxelles, Belgium.

a6401.speaker: Anil Gayan's biography
a6401.speech: His biography says Anil Gayan's ancestors migrated from India when the island was a British colony.

a6401.speaker: African Union Commission (AUC)
a6401.speech: During a series of summits, conferences and meetings, the AUC reiterated the continuing growth of multiple democratic challenges with a wider negative impact across the continent, and particularly itemized military takeovers that have become a distinctive feature (or accepted norm) of regime change in West Africa.

a6401.speaker: Researchers (unnamed)
a6401.speech: Have reminded the African Union and ECOWAS to invoke the African Convention for the Elimination of Mercenary, which went into effect in 1985, prohibiting states from allowing mercenaries into their territories; the researcher further called for addressing promptly 'malign influences' and 'political manipulations', and bringing back the "AU Master Roadmap (AUMR) of Practical Steps to Silencing the Guns in Africa" adopted in 2017.

a6401.speaker: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) report (re-issued February 2022)
a6401.speech: According to the report, UNDP has seriously recommitted its partnerships and opportunities to furthering the Silencing the Guns agenda as a necessary condition for Africa's transformative development, focusing on people, prosperity and peace as the basis for its contributions to the AU's aspirations across Africa.

a6401.speaker: Professor Sergiu Miscoiu, Faculty of European Studies, Babes-Bolyai University, Director of the Centre for International Cooperation and of the Centre for African Studies
a6401.speech: Noted in an article to Global Research that African countries are bound to wake up to a common understanding of the true meaning of their colonial past for the present, and determine their own future existence, and that the leaders and the elites have to engage in development decision-making processes and play their roles as autonomous actors instead of being pawns in global politics.

a6401.speaker: Business & Financial Times (B&FT)
a6401.speech: In mid-July 2024 wrote that the candidates were discreetly campaigning for the top position; the B&FT indicated further that, despite the general qualification being former foreign ministers, and in the case of Odinga being an experienced politician readily preferred by the majority of African leaders, some other distinguishing leadership attitude and approach are necessary and required of the candidate.

a6401.speaker: Professor (Ambassador) Edward Boateng, business executive and politician
a6401.speech: In an opinion article listed criteria for the ideal AU head: an inter-generational bridge capable of fostering inter-generational dialogue; strong leadership in conflict resolution with a coherent continental strategy; commitment to spearheading institutional reforms, enhancing financial sustainability and streamlining decision-making; driving economic reforms, attracting investment and fostering a business-friendly environment; and promotion of policies that enhance gender equality and provide opportunities for young people.

a6428.speaker: President Donald Trump and Elon Musk
a6428.speech: Say their goal is gutting the six-decade-old aid and development agency in a broader campaign to slash the size of the federal government ; Trump and Musk contend that USAID's work is wasteful and furthers a liberal agenda.

a6428.speaker: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols
a6428.speech: Rejected pleas in a lawsuit from employees to keep temporarily blocking the government's plan, allowing the administration to move forward with its plan to pull thousands of USAID staffers off the job in the United States and around the world.

a6428.speaker: U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols
a6428.speech: Said he was satisfied by Trump administration assurances that workers abroad would be allowed to stay in their jobs while on leave beyond the 30 days even if they chose to remain overseas; his ruling also cleared the way for the administration to start the clock on a planned 30-day deadline for USAID staffers and their families to return home if they want their travel paid for by the government.

a6428.speaker: USAID (notices to staffers)
a6428.speech: The agency said in the notices to staffers that it was beginning a firing process called reduction in force that would eliminate 2,000 U.S.-based jobs; a version of the notice posted later on USAID's website put the number of positions to be eliminated lower, at 1,600.

a6428.speaker: USAID (notice issued Sunday)
a6428.speech: USAID's notice Sunday said it was "committed to keeping its overseas personnel safe" and pledged not to cut off USAID staffers abroad from agency systems and other support.

a6428.speaker: Pete Marocco, USAID deputy administrator (Trump appointee running USAID)
a6428.speech: Has indicated he plans to keep about 600 mostly U.S.-based staffers on the job in the meantime, in part to arrange travel for USAID staffers and families abroad.

a6428.speaker: Lawsuits by government workers' unions, USAID contractors and others
a6428.speech: Say the administration lacks the constitutional authority to eliminate an independent agency or congressionally funded programs without lawmakers' approval.

a6428.speaker: A different judge in a second lawsuit tied to USAID
a6428.speech: Said this past week that the administration had kept withholding foreign aid despite his order temporarily blocking the funding freeze and must restore the funding to programs worldwide.

a6428.speaker: Dismissed USAID contractors/workers
a6428.speech: Workers noted that the blanket nature of the notification letters to USAID contractors, excluding the names or positions of those receiving them, could make it difficult for the dismissed workers to get unemployment benefits.

a6428.speaker: Foreign (overseas) USAID staffers
a6428.speech: Fear that continued problems with funding flows and the gutting of most of the headquarters staff will make a safe and orderly return difficult, especially those with children in school, houses to sell and ill family members.

a6555.speaker: Global health and development chiefs (in New York)
a6555.speech: Said that immunising children against preventable diseases is critical to achieving United Nations-led goals to reduce child deaths.

a6555.speaker: Health ministers, donors and the heads of UN agencies (at an event hosted by UNICEF, the Republic of Kenya and the GAVI Alliance)
a6555.speech: Called for the introduction of new vaccines that can dramatically reduce deaths due to diarrhoea and pneumonia, the two biggest killers of children under five.

a6555.speaker: Dr Rose Mugo, Kenya's Minister of Public Health and Sanitation
a6555.speech: Said her country's expanded immunisation programme has reduced deaths among children from 115 per 1,000 live births in 2003 to 75 per 1,000 live births today - a 35% reduction ; "When we are able to introduce new vaccines against diarrhoea and pneumonia we are confident that the number will drop even further."

a6555.speaker: Dr Guillermo Gonzalez, Nicaragua's former health minister and current Special Advisor to the President
a6555.speech: Said his country was reaching up to 95% of children with routine immunisation ; "Since we introduced the rotavirus vaccine three years ago we have observed 35% to 40% reductions in mortality."

a6555.speaker: Margaret Chan, Director-General of the World Health Organisation
a6555.speech: "Vaccines are one of the most cost-effective health interventions and one of the best buys. We appeal to the generosity of donors 'open your purses'." ; "Diarrhoea and pneumonia are the two biggest killers of children. If you invest (in these new vaccines) you can save millions."

a6555.speaker: Government donors from Norway, the United Kingdom and the United States
a6555.speech: Also pledged to keep supporting GAVI's global immunisation effort.

a6555.speaker: Andrew Mitchell, MP, the United Kingdom's Secretary of State for International Development
a6555.speech: Said it was a "global scandal" that children were still dying from vaccine-preventable diseases, and donors needed to do more ; "We don't want to balance our budgets on the backs of the poorest countries of the world. Immunisation is undoubtedly one of the best buys in global health, and GAVI is one of the most effective ways of achieving Millennium Development Goal Four. GAVI is focused on results - that is at the heart of our approach to development."

a6555.speaker: Amie Batson, Deputy Assistant Administrator of the US Agency for International Development (USAID)
a6555.speech: Spoke about the need for smart spending: "Through the Global Health Initiative, the United States is committed to targeting increased resources in a more effective and efficient way. We need creative new approaches to reach the millions of children who are not immunised because, at the end of the day, we will be judged by the lives we save, not the money we spend."

a6555.speaker: GAVI Alliance
a6555.speech: Said that decisions made by donor nations now will determine the fate of as many as 4.2 million of the poorest children in the poorest nations - the ones who are most likely to die in the next five years if they don't receive the vaccines that can save their lives.

a6555.speaker: GAVI Alliance partners, which include UNICEF and WHO
a6555.speech: Say they will build on the successes of the Alliance's first decade, when they delivered vaccines against life-threatening diseases to more than 250 million children, an investment that is expected to save 5.4 million lives.

a6555.speaker: Experts
a6555.speech: Predict that the introduction of the two vaccines can eventually save the lives of one million children per year.

a6564.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a6564.speech: Has pledged to ensure that Chiradzulu District is developed in a way that reflects its historical significance; Chakwera expressed his desire to transform the district into a 'new Blantyre' ; "This is why, three years ago, I launched a nationwide initiative to establish schools of excellence, aiming to equip Malawians in every district with the capacity to utilise the resources available to them for development and progress. One of these schools of excellence will be the Chilembwe School of Excellence, which will be built here in Chiradzulu. It will include a football academy for both boys and girls, with a state-of-the-art stadium featuring facilities for football, netball, basketball, volleyball, athletics and boxing" ; He added that four months ago, he engaged a group of investors from Italy, who are now preparing to bring the necessary resources to develop the Chilembwe School of Excellence ; "This is because Reverend Chilembwe believed that the key to our development progress lies in using education to increase our capacity to utilise the resources we have been blessed with by God."

a6564.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a6564.speech: Also encouraged the people to work hard and contribute to the development of both themselves and the country. He said Chilembwe chose to name his church 'industrial' because he understood that success only comes from hard work and producing goods that can be exported to other countries ; "Over 100 years after Chilembwe's death, no country has developed through foreign aid, politics or having the most educated president. What drives a country's development is industrialisation and the production of our own goods for export, just as Reverend John Chilembwe understood over 100 years ago."

a6564.speaker: Richard Chimwendo Banda, Minister of Local Government, Unity and Culture
a6564.speech: Praised the President for apparently continuing to uphold Chilembwe's vision ; "The President has ensured that development is spread across the country. Upon realising that Malawians need a better life, he has been there for them in times of need. He has, among other things, built hospitals and revived railway transportation to improve the lives of ordinary Malawians."

a6564.speaker: Wilson Mitambo, PIM (Providence Industrial Mission) President
a6564.speech: Commended the authorities for what he called their vision to develop Chiradzulu District and PIM. He also urged the President to consider holding more events in honour of the late missionary, rather than limiting them to just the Chilembwe Day commemorations.

a6624.speaker: Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, former President of Ghana
a6624.speech: Has reiterated his stance on reducing Africa's reliance on foreign aid, emphasising the urgent need for economic self-sufficiency. According to him, true independence for African nations hinges on building strong institutions, developing local industries and creating sustainable economic opportunities. "We cannot continue to rely on foreign aid as the foundation of our economies. True independence means strengthening our own institutions, developing our industries and creating opportunities for our people," he said, delivering a speech on Thursday, February 20, 2025 in Abuja, Nigeria, at the launch of the autobiography of General Ibrahim Babangida.

a6624.speaker: Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, former President of Ghana
a6624.speech: Expressed disappointment about the re-emergence of military coup d'etats in West Africa; according to him, up until a few years ago, he had no doubt the region had built consensus that multi-party democracy would be the most suitable form of governance structure for the continent, including West Africa. "I feel a deep sense of disappointment that military coup d'etats have come back in fashion in our region and are seen as the answer to the instability being spread from the Sahel by Jihadist activity and by some as the answer to difficult economic conditions or unpopular government policies," he said. "In a democracy, elections must be free, fair and transparent. Political leaders have a responsibility to respect the will of the people and strengthen institutions that uphold democratic principles," Akufo-Addo added.

a6624.speaker: Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, former President of Ghana
a6624.speech: Urged ECOWAS and African leaders to take proactive measures to reinforce democracy in the Sahel, warning that political instability creates fertile ground for extremism, insecurity and economic decline. He emphasised that Ghana's experience demonstrates both the strengths and vulnerabilities of democratic governance, stressing that the judiciary and electoral bodies must maintain public trust through greater transparency and accountability. ; In his estimation, the work of the leadership of the region and continent with its people has been cut out all over again, and the people must be convinced again that the road to prosperity would be faster and longer-lasting when we are democratic.

a6624.speaker: Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, former President of Ghana
a6624.speech: Praised General Ibrahim Babangida's autobiography, describing it as an insightful account of West Africa's political evolution and a valuable resource for understanding the challenges of leadership. He commended Babangida for offering a candid reflection on his tenure, the complexities of governance, and the lessons that today's leaders can draw from past experiences. According to Akufo-Addo, the book serves as a crucial historical document that provides perspective on how African nations can navigate the delicate balance between democracy and stability. He said the book reminded all that if a civilian, constitutional government felt under constant threat of destabilisation and had to spend far too much time and resources on security, a military government was under even more threat of insecurity, and he added that if it was overwhelming to end poverty and keep food prices down, they are mostly more tolerable when compared with the unpredictable things that hit a government in Africa. "If it is a difficult and exhausting process to come up with a plausible and workable foreign policy for an African country today, it was a bigger nightmare at the time, described in A Journey In Service," he said.

a6677.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) (statement)
a6677.speech: According to UNICEF, half of these 747,000 people are children: "The third cyclone to hit Mozambique in recent months destroyed schools, cutting off access to education for around 20,000 children. An estimated 747,000 people, half of them children, could be affected by the strong winds, torrential rains and flash floods that hit the provinces of Nampula, Niassa and Zambezia this week" ; "The severe flooding is exacerbating the risk of water-borne diseases, including cholera and diarrhoea - major threats to children's lives. Meanwhile, severe damage to the main roads is disrupting the distribution of essential goods" ; UNICEF explains that this comes at a time when over 730,000 Mozambicans were already suffering the devastating impact of tropical cyclones Chido and Dikeledi, which destroyed or damaged more than 150,000 homes, 471 schools and 100 health facilities.

a6677.speaker: Mary Louise Eagleton, UNICEF Representative in Mozambique
a6677.speech: "The impact of Cyclone Jude on hundreds of thousands of children and families already affected by Cyclones Chido and Dikeledi is devastating. Extreme winds and heavy rains have destroyed critical infrastructure and are depriving vulnerable children of essential services."

a6677.speaker: United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)
a6677.speech: The organization said that it is working with various partners and the Government to respond and meet the needs of those affected, "but having already responded to two cyclones in the space of just a few months, we are overwhelmed and urgently need additional resources" ; said the crisis exceeds current resources "in a country where 3.4 million children were already in need of humanitarian assistance, and the current cyclone season could last another six weeks" ; is calling on donors, governments and the international community to urgently increase and maintain funding for education and emergency response efforts "because without immediate intervention, the future of an entire generation of Mozambican children is at risk."

a6735.speaker: Vital Strategies, Economics for Health team at Johns Hopkins University and Research Unit on the Economics of Excisable Products at the University of Cape Town, policy brief “The Future of Health Financing in Africa: The Role of Health Taxes”
a6735.speech: a document that calls for urgent and strategic implementation of excise taxes on harmful products such as tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages. The report makes a compelling case for health taxes as a transformative tool to combat the escalating burden of NCDs, strengthen fragile health systems and generate sustainable domestic revenue, noting that 37 percent of all deaths across Africa are now attributed to NCDs, that official development assistance is in decline and that funding for NCDs remains woefully inadequate.

a6735.speaker: Vital Strategies, Economics for Health team at Johns Hopkins University and Research Unit on the Economics of Excisable Products at the University of Cape Town, policy brief “The Future of Health Financing in Africa: The Role of Health Taxes”
a6735.speech: The report outlines what it calls a “triple win” for African nations: excise taxes reduce consumption of harmful products across income levels while incentivising manufacturers to reformulate products; health taxes provide stable and predictable funding streams; and by reducing preventable diseases and injuries they allow governments to redirect scarce resources. Yet despite these proven benefits, implementation across Africa remains dangerously inadequate, with rates too low to impact affordability or consumption and poor tax design leaving policies vulnerable to inflation and industry manipulation.

a6735.speaker: Vital Strategies, Economics for Health team at Johns Hopkins University and Research Unit on the Economics of Excisable Products at the University of Cape Town, policy brief “The Future of Health Financing in Africa: The Role of Health Taxes”
a6735.speech: The brief also highlights successful case studies from across the continent: South Africa's 2018 excise tax on sugary drinks led to a 29 percent reduction in taxed beverage purchases per person and a 51 percent decrease in sugar intake, raising R5.8 billion (US$319 million) in its first two years; Botswana's 2021 sugar tax generated 100 million Botswana pula (US$8 million) in 2023-24; and Ghana's 2023 tobacco tax increase raised the tax share of retail price from 23 percent in 2020 to 38 percent in 2024, with revenue more than doubling from GHS 82 million (US$5.4 million) in 2021 to over GHS 187 million (US$12 million) in 2023.

a6735.speaker: Dr Mary-Ann Etiebet, CEO and President of Vital Strategies
a6735.speech: “Health taxes on all unhealthy products—including tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks—save lives, reduce health care costs and generate revenue,” she stated. “This brief offers regionally grounded evidence, policy examples and practical guidance to help African governments resist industry interference and implement health taxes that deliver maximum benefit to citizens. It is especially urgent now, as governments face budget deficits, overwhelmed health systems and rising health care costs.”

a6735.speaker: Corne van Walbeek, Director of the Research Unit on the Economics of Excisable Products at the University of Cape Town
a6735.speech: “The structure and design of health taxes matter,” he said. “International best practice shows that specific taxes—levied per pack of cigarettes, per litre of alcohol, or per gram of sugar—are more effective than value-based taxes. These taxes should be increased regularly to account for inflation and real income growth. When well designed and shielded from industry interference, health taxes reduce consumption and provide governments with a reliable revenue stream.”

a6735.speaker: Jeffrey Drope, Ph.D., Research Professor and Director of the Economics for Health team at Johns Hopkins University
a6735.speech: a 50 percent price increase on tobacco, alcohol and sugary beverages could raise $2.1 trillion in five years for low- and middle-income countries, representing 40 percent of their total health spending. “Health taxes are among the most powerful tools we have to tackle the growing burden of preventable disease in Africa,” Drope asserted.

a6735.speaker: Adam Karpati, Senior Vice President of Public Health Programmes at Vital Strategies and co-author of the brief
a6735.speech: “Health taxes are among the most effective public health interventions available to governments to address the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases like cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes,” he said. “Governments around the world are recognising the multiple benefits of health taxes—saving lives, reducing health care costs and raising revenue. All countries should follow suit.”

a6735.speaker: Serah Makka, Executive Director for Africa at ONE
a6735.speech: “Taxes are synonymous with trust,” she said. “Because there’s resistance to price increases—whether elastic or inelastic—the population must be informed about how these funds will be spent. There must be a transparent through-line from the increased taxes to development that can be seen, felt and experienced by citizens. People are open to paying taxes when they see the impact.”

a6837.speaker: Joyce Banda, People’s Party (PP) leader and former Malawi president
a6837.speech: Says she will improve the education and agriculture sectors if they vote for her as the country’s president in the September 16 polls; said her vision is on education, agriculture and health such that she will introduce mobile clinics to reach out to people in hard-to-reach areas with quality medical services; on education, said she would improve education right from primary, and secondary to tertiary and promised to construct hostels in secondary schools and universities to accommodate students; disclosed that 1,300 students are on her bursary in various secondary while the other 1,300 are on her bursary programme in universities on top of 31 students doing master’s degree programs in the United States of America; said she will develop rural areas and will work with local leaders to achieve sustainable rural development; also said she would ensure that civil servants get good salaries and appealed to people who gathered at the rally to vote for her on September 16: “I assure you that l will develop the agriculture sector to ensure food security in the country. Once I voted to power, l will also ensure that civil servants receive good salaries.”

a6837.speaker: Ben Chakhame, People’s Party Secretary General
a6837.speech: Said the party will win in the September 16 elections and assured people that things will improve in the country; faulted other political parties that mobilise young people to cause chaos during political party meetings, saying this is contrary to multi-party democracy.

a6895.speaker: Eyewitnesses (anonymous)
a6895.speech: Said that on the morning of 27 August, attackers opened fire on children tending cattle in Oroto Keble, Arero district, killing seven-year-old Ebisa Dika.

a6895.speaker: Eyewitnesses (anonymous)
a6895.speech: The eyewitnesses said federal forces later intervened, bringing temporary calm to the area.

a6895.speaker: Kiya Godana, chief administrator of Oroto Keble
a6895.speech: Confirmed to local media that the child, a second-grade student, was killed and buried the same day.

a6895.speaker: Residents (of Wachille area)
a6895.speech: Residents reported renewed clashes in the Melka Adi area of Wachille between ethnic Oromo people and armed men from the Somali Region.

a6895.speaker: Borbor town residents
a6895.speech: Confirmed that people displaced from Dhaas have settled there ; They stressed the urgent need for humanitarian assistance, warning that unless the security issues along the East Borana-Somali border are resolved, clashes and displacement will continue.

a7108.speaker: Participants at the African Development Bank Forum
a7108.speech: Agreed that more should be done to tap into and engage the diaspora community and leverage their strengths for Africa's benefit.

a7108.speaker: Akinwumi A. Adesina, African Development Bank President
a7108.speech: In his opening remarks, said that regardless of overseas success, Africans remain tied to the continent of their birth as a source of identity and pride, and consequently the development of Africa must be a priority for all Africans in the diaspora: "The African diaspora has become the largest financier of Africa! And it is not debt; it is 100% gifts or grants, a new form of concessional financing that is the key for livelihood security for millions of Africans," ; "Because the flow of remittances to Africa is high, rising, and stable, it offers huge opportunities to serve as collateral to secure financing for African economies. African countries should securitise remittances to promote investments, especially for infrastructure on the continent."

a7108.speaker: Akinwumi A. Adesina, African Development Bank President
a7108.speech: Urged that Africans living in the Diaspora be given the right to vote in elections in their respective countries; called for ministries to be set up to serve those in the Diaspora: "I implore and encourage African governments to create the conditions for those living and working overseas to contribute meaningfully to national development or, even better, not to leave in the first place."

a7108.speaker: Monique Nsanzabaganwa, Deputy African Union Commission Chairperson
a7108.speech: Recalled that African heads of state committed to engaging the diaspora as far back as 2012 by establishing a database of diaspora professionals, an African Institute for remittances, and an Africa diaspora investment fund, among other initiatives.

a7108.speaker: Wamkele Mene, Secretary General of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) secretariat
a7108.speech: Said remittances offer a window of opportunity for Africa's development against a backdrop of declining foreign direct investment and foreign aid ; cited the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, a collaboration between Afreximbank and the AfCFTA secretariat, which works with Africa's central banks to establish financial market infrastructure for commercial banks, payment service providers, card schemes and other intermediaries to handle payment and settlement service across Africa; said operationalising the AfCFTA, which came into force in January 2021, would ease the way for diaspora communities to invest in Africa.

a7108.speaker: Antonio Vitorino, Director General of the International Organisation for Migration
a7108.speech: Urged African countries to take a proactive approach to their overseas communities: "Governments need to get to know their diaspora; this starts with knowing where the diaspora is located, what their skills and capacities are, and how willing they are to engage in development at home." ; pointed to philanthropic engagement and diaspora tourism as potential areas of mutual interest for African governments and the diaspora.

a7108.speaker: Ambassador Rama Yade, US-based Atlantic Council's Africa and Europe centers
a7108.speech: "Africa is the oldest continent, the youngest continent, and soon to be the largest continent."

a7108.speaker: Romi Bhatia, Senior Advisor for Diaspora Partnerships at USAID
a7108.speech: Said there were still too many headlines in the western media focusing on disease or death and despair in Africa, causing U.S businesses to overemphasize the risk - both real and perceived - across the continent: "Consequently, U.S. companies are missing out on opportunities to build mutually beneficial trade and investment partnerships across the Atlantic."

a7108.speaker: Albert Muchanga, African Union Commissioner for Trade and Industry
a7108.speech: Echoed this: "If others see you invest in Africa and you generate high returns, their risk perception is likely to go down."

a7108.speaker: Albert Muchanga, African Union Commissioner for Trade and Industry
a7108.speech: Stressed that while the African Continental Free Trade Area is critical to deepening pan-African trade, African countries must also be involved in global trade.

a7111.speaker: Pope Francis, 2015 encyclical Laudato Si'
a7111.speech: Emphasised the need for an integral approach to combating environmental degradation and poverty.

a7111.speaker: Islamic leaders, Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change
a7111.speech: Urging Muslims to act as stewards of the planet.

a7310.speaker: United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) (medal award citation)
a7310.speech: Among other things, the personnel were recognised for their valuable contributions to humanitarian assistance initiatives, protection of civilians and ongoing efforts in strengthening the capacity of local enforcement agencies.

a7310.speaker: Chief Supt Bismark Achaab, Contingent Commander of the Ghana Formed Police Unit
a7310.speech: Addressing the parade, urged the contingent to carry forward the lessons they had learnt ; also encouraged them to let their experiences inspire others to serve, to lead by example and to uphold the values of the UN.

a7481.speaker: Authorities of the Nigerian military
a7481.speech: Have revealed that no fewer than 2,190 repentant terrorists have been reintegrated back to the society through its programmes called Operation Safe Corridor since its inception in 2016.

a7481.speaker: Yusuff Ali, Brigadier-General, Coordinator of Operation Safe Corridor
a7481.speech: Disclosed that the number included 27 foreign nationals, who have been repatriated to their respective countries; explained that between July and November 2024, 825 new clients – including 14 foreigners from Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad and Niger – were transferred to the De-radicalization, Rehabilitation, and Reintegration camp for training; added that 22 clients requiring further psychological evaluation were transferred to the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Maiduguri ; “Since the commencement of the Programme in 2016, OPSC has successfully processed 2,190 clients comprising 2,163 Nigerians and 27 foreign nationals from Cameroon, Chad and Niger. All the foreign clients were transferred to their respective national authorities for reintegration. Between July and November 2024, a total of 825 clients were transferred to the DRR Camp to commence training. Amongst them are 14 foreigners from Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad and Niger. It is also important to mention that 22 clients were subsequently transferred to the Federal Neuro Psychiatric Hospital, Maiduguri for further evaluation and management.”

a7481.speaker: Yusuff Ali, Brigadier-General, Coordinator of Operation Safe Corridor
a7481.speech: Told the gathering that the meeting was aimed at finalising strategies for the smooth transfer of rehabilitated clients to state and national authorities for reintegration upon graduation in March 2025.

a7481.speaker: General Christopher Musa, Chief of Defence Staff (represented by Air Vice Marshal Shayi Olatunde, Chief of Defence Policy and Plans)
a7481.speech: Emphasised the importance of proper reintegration to sustain the progress made by OPSC; revealed that over 130,000 insurgents and their family members have surrendered since the programme began, and that currently 789 ex-combatants are undergoing rehabilitation, with 381 expected to graduate in 2025.

a7481.speaker: General Christopher Musa, Chief of Defence Staff
a7481.speech: Called on state governments to facilitate the reintegration process by providing additional support, including security measures to track and monitor the ex-combatants’ progress; reiterated that each graduate would receive personal items and startup packages to help them establish small businesses and start a new life.
